These independent truckers are struggling to survive. They are protesting against the fact that truckers from neighbouring provinces and the United States have invaded Quebec and the Abitibi-Temiscamingue area and are competing unfairly against them.

Mr. Speaker, the federal government has pulled the rug from under Manitoba's culture industry. The budget of the Canada-Manitoba Cultural Industries Development Office, CIDO, has been slashed for 1990, but worse still come March 1991, the Conservative government will withdraw
completely its support of CIDO. There will be nothing left.
The federal government has reneged on the commitment it made when the Canada-Manitoba CIDO was created. This is a major blow to Manitoba's cultural industry and economy. It will kill, for example, a young but successful film industry. Producers and technicians will leave the province in order to do their work elsewhere, resulting in the loss of nearly 200 direct jobs. Manitoba's economy will lose more than $7 million in related broad-based economic spin-offs.
CIDO was a success. Why tamper with success? Once again this government is showing its lack of interest in Manitoba and western Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the government has been trying to pass Meech, not by convincing Canadians, but by threatening them. These threats have not worked. Instead, they have only proven that Meech cannot be sold on its merits.
The threat is Quebec's separation. This is a real issue and may be dealt with eventually, but passing Meech will not make eventual separation any less likely. Defeating Meech will not make it any more likely.
I urge the province of Quebec to recognize that the rejection of Meech Lake is not a rejection of the people of Quebec, but a rejection of the flawed Prime Minister-Bourassa approach to constitution making.
I call upon the Prime Minister of Canada to accept responsibility for the constitutional chaos into which his Meech Lake initiative has led this country and to resign.

Perhaps NATO recognized that 40,000 over-flights a year would be destructive to the Innu way of life. Perhaps NATO recognizes that changes in Europe and a reduction in international tensions made the test facility obsolete.
Flowever, it is an unfortunate comment on leadership in Canada that under the Conservative government and in the face of east-west tensions, the Prime Minister himself could ignore the Innu and their land, and insist on proceeding with Canada's bid for the base.
The cancellation of the base does not mean an end to the 7,000 over-flights a year already conducted out of Goose Bay. Under agreement they will continue for another six years.
If Canada wants to create employment in the Happy Valley-Goose Bay area, it should embark on negotiations to settle aboriginal claims in the region. Those settlements result in economic independence for native communities, a repatriation of capital to the region, and more jobs for natives and non-natives alike.
If Canada could show sufficient respect for the Innu, it would abandon all low-level test flights in Labrador now.

Mr. Speaker, during the fall of 1986, 11 first ministers met in Edmonton and determined that the next logical step in the constitutional process was to conclude arrangements that would honourably permit Quebec to return to the Canadian family.
Such provisions were achieved several months later at Meech Lake under the inspired and persuasive leadership of our Prime Minister. For the only time in Canadian history 11 first ministers came together in historic agreement.
Prior to ratification of that agreement, elections brought new first ministers to three provinces. They were not a part of the process and concluded that their agendas were more important. But without the prior ratification of the Meech Lake Accord, with or without a companion resolution, there may be no future agendas.
May 23, 1990

Atlantic Canada can ill-afford the political and economic uncertainty that the loss of the Meech Lake Accord will bring. I urge Premiers Wells and McKenna to serve Atlantic Canada's interest, to ensure Canada remains strong by passing and putting Meech behind us in order that we can all look forward with optimism to future constitutional and economic agendas.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the House passed a resolution condemning and deploring racism and intolerance in Canadian society, as reflected in acts of vandalism in cemeteries.
The House has spoken, Mr. Speaker, but I wonder whether this gesture should not go further. A recent study by B'nai Brith points to a 57 per cent increase in racist incidents against Canada's racial minorities last year.
Yesterday, an article in The Gazette reported a series of racist and violent incidents in Quebec and Ontario which occured between May 12 and May 20. In one incident, five "skinheads" assaulted a black youth on Saint-Laurent Boulevard in Montreal. Are these incidents symptomatic of a deeper, underlying malaise? Why now? Why cemeteries? Who are these unknowns who perpetrate such terrible acts? Were these incidents orchestrated?
Mr. Speaker, our responsibility to the victims bids us to ask serious questions.

Mr. Speaker, I was privileged to serve on the committee that studied the companion resolution to the Meech Lake Accord. It was an experience of politics at its best; three political parties working together for the good of Canada.
I would like to share a personal experience with the House of Commons. While in Vancouver, Mr. Glen Cowan gave testimony before the committee. He and I met later for a private discussion.
This fine, well-read and deeply committed Canadian told me that four decades ago, he and four of his friends voluntarily left for a theatre of war a wide ocean and a continent away.
They risked their lives in the name of Canada. Three of those five men never returned. They are, in the name of freedom and Canada, buried in foreign soil.
Mr. Cowan himself was twice seriously wounded. Every day that he did battle, he knew the great risk involved.
He then, with a burden that comes with painful knowledge, said to me: "If we young people were willing to lay down our lives for Canada, then surely these hold-out provinces can make a political sacrifice in the name of nation-building."
Sir, I concur. The torch is ours to hold high. The most magnificent nation on earth must not fail.

Oral Questions FISHERIES
Mr. Francis G. LeBIanc (Cape Breton Highlands -
Canso): Mr. Speaker, yesterday 38 trawlermen travelled by bus from Canso to Ottawa to speak out on the crisis facing their community. They had three messages for this government, and in particular for the Minister of Fisheries.
First, the central problem of the Atlantic fisheries is not too many fishermen chasing too few fish. It is too many powerful fishing boats destroying too many fish at sea. This scandalous practice is occurring at the same time that fish plants in our coastal communities are closing for want of fish to process. This practice has got to stop.
Second, the people of Canso are not responsible for the crisis in which they now find themselves. Canso is a victim of the murky scheme to use declining quotas in the northern cod stock as a pretext for rationalizing this community out of existence.
Third, the solution to the Canso problem is simple. Give back to its fishermen their rightful share of the quota taken from them by National Sea's departure and ensure that the trawlers continue to fish from the Canso port.
This is within the power of the Minister of Fisheries to achieve. It is what the people of Canso have asked for from the beginning. They and I will accept nothing less.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to express my heartfelt sadness at the anger, fear and intolerance I am seeing and hearing in my country, Canada.
Goodness knows our history is not without blemish. I believe we have tried to learn from our past, and we have tried to build a better Canada for our future generations. I wonder if we have suddenly stopped caring and trusting each other. Why are we responding to perceived fears and threats to our national unity rather than reaching out and embracing the one vehicle that will unite us, the Meech Lake Accord?
By accepting Meech Lake, we do not lose any of the provisions that exist in the Constitution Act, 1982. Instead, we gain by including Quebec in the Canadian family where she belongs.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. This government is caught in a crisis mentality. Crises often have a negative impact. People tend to panic. We must not lose sight of our objective which is to resolve the constitutional impasse. This must not be done in secret, if we want to end this panic situation.
My question for the Prime Minister is as follows: Could the Prime Minister inform the House of the contents of the text proposed by Senator Murray?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I would like to inform my hon. friend that there is no panic situation in Canada. We have experienced some human problems. The New Democrats think that is funny. We have had a number of problems, a number of challenges of that nature. This happens in a government, but of course the New Democrats have had no experience of the responsibility of running a government. From time to time, prime ministers or governments must- Mr. Speaker, I vigou-rously deny any suggestion that there is a problem, a panic situation in this country. We have human problems and we have political problems. We are faced with a major challenge at the constitutional level. There has been a long debate on the question.
I said it yesterday and I repeat it today: Three years ago, the Government of Quebec signed a document, with all the other provinces and the federal government, to make it part of Canada, and of the Canadian Constitution, a participation to which all parties freely consented, which would make our country united, something we have all wanted since 1981. Finally, we had a document on the basis of which we could all say that we had a strong, united Canada. All Canadians could believe that since the premiers of all the provinces and the Prime Minister of Canada signed that document, Quebecers
May 23, 1990

and Canadians could expect to see this document ratified.
That has not been the case. Since then, three provinces have repudiated the signatures of their premiers who had previously given their consent, which creates a serious problem for Canada. We, the government and the opposition parties, are trying to find a formula that will make it possible for Quebec to again become part of the Canadian family, on terms and conditions that are honourable. I have received no recommendations in writing from Senator Murray. I have received suggestions that will help us maintain the dialogue, continue the dialogue, in order to try to break this constitutional impasse, because I think that all Canadians want to see Quebec become part of our Canadian family again, once and for all.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Prime Minister.
I suggest to the Prime Minister that the country does not need a history lesson from him but some leadership.

If he wants to refer to history, then I say to him that surely we have learned something from the process which has taken place.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. friend for the question. speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:

speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, May 22, consideration of Bill C-43, an act respecting abortion, as reported (without amendment) from a legislative committee, and on Motions Nos. 4, 5, 10, 12, 13, 14, 16, 17A, 17B, 19, 22 and 24.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-43, an act respecting abortion is one which deals with a subject that divides members of this House and the people of Canada.
Some people want strong legislation, others have said that the government should not even legislate in this area. I do not agree with the contention that we should not make laws on abortion. To me, it is essential that we legislate on the very definition of life and being, as well as on the rights associated with our being. Nothing could be more fundamental.
As it is presented, Bill C-43 is not acceptable. Unless it is substantially amended, I cannot support it. When the bill was first introduced, I spoke at length on my concerns relating to this issue. These concerns involve my belief that we cannot discuss abortion until we define life as beginning at conception, my desire for better support systems for women with crisis pregnancies, the need for preventive counselling and support, and my belief that there should be a major reorganization of our
May 23, 1990

basic philosophies towards the supporting and nurturing of families.
I do not want to repeat these arguments today, but I do want to speak briefly on the proposed amendments. I think it is important that I set out the reasons for the decisions I will be making when these amendments are brought to a vote.
I would like to deal with the proposed amendments in the order that they will be presented for voting. First, let me say that I will reject Motion No. 3 out of hand. In my view, this amendment attempts to change one of the most fundamental aspects of Bill C-43. It would allow abortion on demand and limit the application of this law.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. The member on the opposite side is speaking to an amendment that was never moved. It has been withdrawn. He is speaking to Motion No. 3 and I would suggest that is out of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member is on debate so he can speak on any motion. I am sure he is going to get to one of the other motions. If he wants to speak to Motion No. 3 he can. It is debate. The hon. member for Calgary North.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate very much my hon. colleague's comments. I was not aware of that, and I would be pleased to discuss other motions that have been proposed.
Motions Nos. 4 and 22 attempt to increase dramatically the punishments that would be incurred by those who would illegally commit abortions. I have grave concerns over this type of amendment. To approve it would be to signal that our interests are in punishment and revenge. This is not and should not be the case.
As I have said before, the key issue is the definition of the beginning of life and the careful, compassionate balancing of rights from that point onwards. Emphasis on extreme punishment is a vindictive approach that fails to consider the enormous emotional and psychological stresses that are involved. It is inconsistent with a caring society and also inconsistent with other parts of the
Government Orders
Criminal Code. Therefore, I cannot support these amendments.
Motion No. 5 would limit the performance of abortions to medical practitioners. It would not allow the procedure to be performed by nurses or assistants under the supervision of a doctor. Although I believe that the amendment would have little actual effect on the number of abortions performed, I would like to support it. Doctors have a choice whether or not to participate in abortions. Their employees do not, nor do the employees of hospitals. Although this amendment tries to relieve nurses from having to actually perform abortions, they would still be forced to assist. The distinction is too fine and would not be upheld in the courts. I will not support this amendment, although I support its intent.
Motion No. 10 attempts to remove the health of the mother from consideration and leave the life of the mother as the only criterion for determining whether or not an abortion should proceed. I sympathize with the intent of this motion but I do not believe it is always possible for a doctor to determine exactly whether life or just health is at stake. I also do not believe that this amendment is constitutionally valid.
For these reasons, I will vote against Motion No. 10 in the hope that other motions, specifically Motions Nos. 12 and 13 will carry.
Motion No. 12 clarifies for me that there must be a serious threat to life and health for an abortion to be considered. Although I am not certain that Motion No.
12	would be of much use without Motion No. 13, I will support it.
It is important to point out that I consider Motion No.
13	to be the key to amending Bill C-43 successfully. This amendment limits the procedure of abortion to those cases in which no other medically acceptable treatment is available to alleviate the risk. It clarifies the issue that rights must be balanced. The test is the availability of medical procedures for the protection of the life and health of the mother. This amendment will receive my support.
Motion No. 14 would remove the definition of health from the bill. I do not consider this appropriate as I believe physicians may not always be able to distinguish between serious health and life risks. Although I believe the definition must be left in, I also believe it should be

May 23, 1990
Government Orders
strengthened. Therefore, I will vote against Motion No. 14 and for Motion No. 16, which I believe places clear and acceptable limitations on the definition of health. If Motion No. 16 fails, I will support Motion No. 17B rather than 17A, as I believe that Motion 17B leaves less room for interpretation of the word "health".
Motion No. 19 attempts to introduce the concept of a solid body of scientific knowledge into the definition of the medical practitioner's opinion. I have real concern for the ability of the courts to interpret such a clause. It would, in my opinion, invite numerous court challenges. I will therefore vote against this motion.
Motion No. 20 causes me a great deal of concern. The intent of the motion is to include in the definition of abortion, methods of birth control which work after initial conception but before implantation. I will not support this motion as I believe that deleting this clause will result in enormous confusion and uncertainty in matters relating to birth control. I strongly support birth control as the most effective method of reducing the perceived need for abortion.
The last amendment before us is Motion No. 24, which proposes to gut Bill C-43 so that there is, in fact, no law on abortion. Although I may disagree with the bill as amended, or not amended at this point, I will not support this motion.
I consider it essential that we define life in our laws. I believe that Bill C-43 does this by recognizing that abortion is fundamentally wrong. Although the definitions are not what I might like, I must reaffirm the duty of Parliament to legislate on matters of morality. I will therefore vote against this amendment.
Finally, I wish to say to my colleagues, to the Prime Minister, and to the Minister of Justice, how much I respect and appreciate the way in which the process of debate on this bill has been handled. I am well aware of the deep divisions that exist and of the enormous compromises already made on this issue in order to bring a bill, any bill, before this House.
In the final analysis, should I find that 1 have to vote against this bill, I will do so with great reluctance and not in any sense to criticize or condemn those who have come to a different conclusion. It is my sincere hope that
amendments will be made that will enable me to support this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I listened carefully to the comments of the member on the opposite side because I think he hit the nail on the head when he stated that this bill and the amendments fail to discuss the true issue. We as Canadians and as parliamentarians have to face it. When does life begin and when do we, as a society, propose to protect it?
We are talking about amendments to Bill C-43. The amendment is designed to improve the bill in some way. I would like to talk about my views on the amendments, whether they achieve what they set out to achieve, and second, on the circumstances surrounding the amendment process of Bill C-43. In order to determine whether an amendment aids or improves a particular bill, we have to look at the bill. At the beginning, I want to say that in my analysis, Bill C-43 is fatally flawed and totally unconstitutional, regardless of which side of the issue you are on, or whether you even have a side.
I say this simply because the Supreme Court of Canada the past summer in the Chantal Daigle case set out quite clearly what is the responsibility of parliamentarians. It made a statement that the foetus has absolutely no protection under Canadian law at the present time. It went further and said that the people of Canada and those who represent them in the House of Commons can, if they so decide, protect the foetus. If they wish to do so, it is fundamental that the protection be explicitly spelled out in legislation, not implicitly.
Otherwise, the bill will be unconstitutional. We did not follow that advice in Bill C-43 because there is no statement as to why abortion is being re-criminalized. There is no indication in the bill why we are putting abortion back into the Criminal Code. The first thing I look for in an amendment is to see if this fundamental flaw in the legislation is dealt with. Unfortunately, as I see the 12 amendments, the flaw is not addressed.
There is no amendment dealing with a definition of life. There is no amendment stating why the procedure of abortion is contrary to the accepted norms of society in the views of the proposers of the bill. How then can those amendments improve the bill as it now stands in its unconstitutional form, as I see it?
May 23, 1990

That brings me to the second point about the amendment process, that is, the circumstances surrounding the amendment. We were told that we would have a free vote, that we would be able to exercise our consciences on this very emotional and divisive issue which has torn the country apart and has set families one against the other. That is what we were told by our Prime Minister. He indicated in the 1988 general election that he would allow a free vote.
Instead, he has committed a fraud on the Canadian people by insisting not on allowing a free vote but that his cabinet ministers abandon conscience in favour of loyalty; then further, to send the message quite clearly that absolutely no amendments whatsoever were to be considered with respect to this bill. Regardless of what the amendment might be, regardless of whether it improved or made constitutional or changed in any way the intent of the bill, there were no amendments to be considered. The message is clear and totally contrary to the promises made by the Prime Minister that members of this House would be able to view this legislation on the basis of conscience and vote in accordance with their conscience.
Cabinet ministers are struggling in this House and indicating their dilemma, indicating that they feel that they are in effect coerced into voting in favour of Bill C-43, in fact voting against all of the amendments. This is a free vote? How can we have amendments which benefit the legislation in the face of coercion? I say that we cannot do so. It is simply impossible.
The amendments have made efforts to improve the bill in the eyes of the mover. I do not propose to go through each and every amendment. I simply wish to state that in the absence of a grappling by this country and by this Parliament of the fundamental issue, which is "Does an abortion kill a human being?", and then depending on the answer, struggle with what we do to prevent that or to allow it, and in the absence of struggling with whether or not life begins at conception or some time subsequent, we cannot deal with this bill. Therefore, I see no amendments which can save this bill constitutionally or make it logically flow to answer that question.
Having said that, it seems to me that Motion No. 10 makes an attempt to indicate the revulsion that society
Government Orders
has for the procedure of abortion, except when it is necessary to save a human life. It does not deal with, nor does the bill deal with, why we have this revulsion, why an abortion brings on different feelings than a tonsillectomy or an appendectomy, but at least it attempts to define and limit when we are going to have the procedure of abortion.
Unfortunately, in my view, even the amendment is broadly worded. If we look at the amendment as proposed it reads, and I will only read that portion which is being amended: "If the abortion were not induced, the life of the female person would be likely to be threatened."
It seems to me that the intent of the bill is that if the life of the female person is threatened, the procedure should be performed. For what purpose? To save the life. Not to destroy a life, but to save a life. However, to leave the phrase "likely to be threatened", I believe totally removes any proposed protection that Motion No. 10 would wish to bring to the bill.
Accordingly, I sympathize with the intent, as I see it, of Motion No. 10. Because I sympathize with the intent of Motion No. 10 and because I feel that Bill C-43, whether or not it is amended is, based on these amendments and based on its present structure, unconstitutional, I cannot support the bill or any of the amendments.
However, I want to make it clear that when I do vote for Motion No. 10, it will be to show that I am in favour of the spirit behind the motion which was the protection of life, the protection of the life in the womb and the protection of the life of the female person whose life would be threatened if the procedure were not performed.
All of the other amendments do not deal with the fundamental issue, which is the question of life. Therefore, I will not be supporting any of those amendments, with the exception of Motion No. 10.

Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to speak again on this important subject. Although my position in the House has changed, my position on this particular item has not changed.
I would like to reiterate that I appreciate very much the method by which this bill was arrived at. The consultation among the caucus and the discussions with many people in the committee was a good way of formulating legislation. However, I have a problem with

May 23, 1990
Government Orders
the legislation in that I believe that it has failed in that it does not protect the unborn.
If we read the legislation, there is absolutely nothing that protects the unborn foetus which, of course, is helpless. I believe that as a Parliament we need to recognize the relative rights of the mother and those of the foetus.
There has been some question about whether any amendments to this bill will be constitutionally correct. I suggest that if our Constitution does not protect the helpless in our society, perhaps we should take a look at that Constitution.
It was clear from the Supreme Court decisions the two previous speakers mentioned, where the Supreme Court cast down the previous abortion law, that there should be some protection somewhere for the foetus.
I would like to quote from the Legal Aspects of Abortion from the research branch of the Library of Parliament which states: "Apart from the obvious fact that there is no longer an enforceable federal prohibition against abortions in Canada, the full import of the court's ruling in the Morgentaler case is as yet unknown." The majority of the court did not rule that women had an unconditional right to abortion under the Charter. On the contrary, it merely concluded that the existing provisions on abortions were set so as to impair irretrievably a pregnant woman's Section 7 rights.
All five justices comprising the majority acknowledged the interest of the foetus was deserving of constitutional recognition under Section 1. Three expressly stated that the law restricting abortions might yet be consistent with the Charter where at some point during the pregnancy the state's interests in protecting the foetus might be sufficiently compelling to override the rights that women otherwise might have under the Charter.
Although the justices did not indicate when this compelling state interest might crystallize, Madam Justice Wilson, who wrote the strongest judgment against the existing abortion law, made the following comments: 'The precise point in the development of the foetus at which the state's interest in its protection becomes compelling, I leave to the informed judgment of the legislature which is in a position to receive guidance on the subject from all relevant disciplines. It seems to me
however that it might fall somewhere in the second trimester".
We could go on with that, but it does show that the Supreme Court indicated that there should be some type of protection for that foetus.
A lot of the debate and the discussions throughout the country centre around the idea of when does life actually begin. Does it begin at conception? Does it begin at the age of viability when the baby or the foetus can live outside the womb? As we read the literature, examine precedents in court, and even medical opinions, it is very difficult to come to a conclusion as to when this actually does occur.
A lot of it really depends on our own attitude toward the unborn. I remember in particular a case of mine in the past where a woman went into labour at 24 weeks, just at the borderline of so-called viability. In the case room there were three doctors, two nurses and an anaesthetist. The baby was born weighing under two pounds and was taken to the Vancouver General Hospital. The baby went through six months of intensive care. Today this baby is a very beautiful teenager. At the same time that the struggle was going on to maintain the life of this baby, an abortion was being performed in the operating room of this same hospital.
There was an instance last summer where a foetus of the same age was aborted that could have been saved. It could have been a life that carried on.
Our attitudes are very important in determining our judgment and the positions that we take.
I believe that our society must defend the defenceless. I cannot think of anything more defenceless than an unborn baby.
I was very impressed during deliberations of the legislative committee by a submission from the Families and Friends of the Handicapped on Bill C-43. I would like to quote from the submission that they made to the committee.
These people represented a number of types of handicapped children. There were also parents who had adopted handicapped children and adults with handicaps. In their brief they stated: "If society takes the position that a disability is a sufficient reason to deny treatment to a child or is grounds for ending that child's life before birth through abortion, society is making a
May 23, 1990

profound and dangerous statement about all human life. Society is saying that the lives of the unborn are second-class and not worth defending, that the life of a disabled person is not really worth living".
They further stated: "Are we expected to believe that a society which sanctions death before birth is a society which will recognize and respect the rights, the aspirations and the human dignities of persons with a disability? It is not just eugenic abortions which represent a threat to the disabled. Any abortion law which sanctions the killing of children poses an equal threat. Such a law establishes the principle that the value of a human life is to be determined by its value to other persons" and I think that that is a very significant statement. "A permissive abortion law embraces the principle that one group of human beings can be declared to be of secondary value and to be disposable. If the unborn can be so designated, so can the disabled".
Because this submission was from a group of disabled people, many of their comments are in that vein.
"Bill C-43 represents an attack upon the efforts of the disabled to obtain equality in society and win the dignity and respect to which they are entitled. The bill would allow abortion for the widest possible reasons. It would enshrine in law a principle that the lives of some may be destroyed for the convenience of others".
There are many points in their brief. I would like to make one last quotation: "We have also reached a crucial moment because of our frequently expressed belief in the equality of everyone is now put to the test. If we say that some people are more equal than others, that the lives of some can be destroyed for the sake of others, then we have abandoned our cherished principles of equality".
Although that is a particular point of view, we need to take note of it and see where this law could possibly lead in the future.
There are some other problems with the law as it stands. I would bring forth the brief from the Canadian Medical Association which opposes Bill C-43. It is particularly concerned about the first amendments we are dealing with, Motions Nos. 4 and 22.
Government Orders
The CMA brief points out that "the bill singles out abortion as the only specified medical act to attract Criminal Code sanctions", and I think we need to ask why that should be. The CMA believes that such treatment is inappropriate and abortion should be treated and controlled under the same statutes that apply to other medical acts.
The CMA further comments: "The inclusion of abortion in the Criminal Code threatens the nature of the physician-patient relationship. The ultimate effect of this bill would be to confer legal entitlement to abortion, but at the expense of access to the service. The bill creates a conceptual nightmare and the bill is vague in its intent".
There are various problems with the bill. It does not protect the innocent or the unborn. It puts the medical fraternity at a distinct disadvantage. They are the only people under this bill that in any way are at risk for carrying out their duties, and of course they are concerned about future access.

Mr. Speaker, to say that this is a complex and difficult issue would be a fantastic understatement. Every individual Canadian has wrestled with it and has had to come to grips with this very personal and difficult moral issue. Some say you cannot legislate morality, but I believe that we must try.
This issue challenges the basic question of what we believe in as individuals and as a society. This issue speaks to rights, freedoms, choices, responsibilities, and obligations of the individual and of society.
Throughout the 1980s Canadians have watched a difference of opinion grow and fester into a raging debate that has deeply divided many Canadians. It has created countless front page headlines on dragged out court battles, demonstrations involving thousands of Canadians, and repeated arrests.
The debate on abortion is really a debate on values, rights, and obligations. It is a debate that has grown into a conflict where both sides have confronted each other frequently in the courtroom. The repeated legal battles saw the conflict mount and result in the Supreme Court of Canada striking down the law governing abortion.
Now this painful and divisive issue has been put by the Supreme Court into the hands of Parliament to be resolved. As members of Parliament we are elected by

May 23, 1990
Government Orders
Canadians to make political decisions, decisions that will benefit society as a whole while respecting the rights of the individual. Parliament must attempt to resolve this conflict in Canadian society.
As we have been debating Bill C-43 in the House of Commons, my hon. colleagues have risen to give their thoughtful opinions on the abortion issue. While I may not agree with all of them, I do respect their differing opinions.
This conflict in Canadian society is created by deeply divided views on abortion. Each side is demanding that the law governing abortion protect differing rights. One group demands that the rights of the unborn be recognized and protected under the law. Another group demands just as strongly that the rights of women be upheld and protected. The people of Canada wait for leadership from Parliament to resolve this conflict.
Bill C-43 has been characterized by the government as a compromise, but how can the government claim to have covered the middle ground when it has done nothing to address the fundamental problems at the root of the conflict? The government has done nothing to address the rights of the unborn, the key issue at the core of the debate.
It is the duty and responsibility of the government to draft a bill that is good for Canadian society by trying to bring an end to the conflict surrounding the debate. I believe this bill has failed the test and will fail again.
The committee that sought to hear the opinions of Canadians and groups met for a number of weeks and heard expert witnesses. I think it is fair to say that most of those groups representing a number of viewpoints have all said that this bill has failed the test and should be rejected. Nowhere in the bill does it speak about life. It speaks about protecting the life and health of a woman, and I am fully supportive of that. However the bill is frighteningly silent about life and the meaning of life, especially the life and the rights of the unborn.
Deep in our hearts we all know that life begins at conception, that a living cell is nurtured within the womb of a mother until such time as it can sustain itself outside the protective life sustaining system of the mother.
Advances in medical technology now make it possible for that living human being to be sustained outside the protective womb as early as 19 weeks, and who knows where we go from there. I am proud to have in my riding a world renowned hospital, St. Joseph's Hospital, dedicated to this end.
My point is that as a society and as individuals we all rejoice at the miracle of birth and life. As a society, once a person is born, we devote our total attention and resources to protecting that life. We expend millions of dollars and would expend anything it takes to protect and enhance life. As a society, we do that from birth to death. Therefore, it is implausible to me that if we believe in life after birth, that we would not do everything possible to ensure that the rights of yet to be born human beings should also be protected and enhanced.
If this bill with certain amendments were to be passed, especially those that seek to speak to life and the rights of the unborn, we will be saying that we believe in something. For, if we do not believe in life, what do we believe in?
Therefore I will be supportive of those amendments that seek to restrict abortions and take into consideration the life and the serious health implications of the mother.
Life should be the rule and abortion should be the exception, and not the other way around. Society should understand and know not only what a law says, but what it means. It must have a value system built in.
The exceptions where an abortion should be permissible should only be when the life of the woman is in danger and the medical risks are substantial and serious.
It must be clear to those seeking an abortion and to those medical practitioners called upon to perform an abortion that it should be the exception and not the rule.
Having said that, it is also imperative that as a society and as a government that supportive community resources be encouraged and supported and that other governmental policies and programs are in place to reinforce our commitment that we intend to encourage, support, and assist women, specifically, who have to make this heart-rending, excruciating and personal decision.
May 23, 1990

The community and government must play a very positive, substantial and supportive role up front, and not as an after the fact matter.
In addition, I have some grave reservations as to the criminal implications of this bill. I voted against Bill C-43 at second reading because I felt that this bill was seriously flawed from a number of standpoints and, if certain amendments were not passed to ensure a proper balance of competing rights, that I could not and would not support this bill at third reading.
I have listened to Canadians and my constituents for almost 16 months on this fundamental issue. I do not believe their views are respected and reflected in Bill C-43 as written. This bill has failed to achieve the delicate balance sought by this government and has failed to meet the challenge laid out by the Supreme Court to Parliament to recognize the rights of the unborn.

Mr. Speaker, I volunteered to sit on the legislative committee on abortion, although I was quite aware it would be a very difficult and onerous committee, because I felt it was important that our caucus have female representation. Although I feel this issue is important to men, it directly affects women. As a woman representative in this Parliament, I felt I had a special interest in representing women on it.
Second, it is important that we in our particular caucus have representation from the centre, from the people who do not have extreme views of those who think that abortion should only be permitted in very rare instances affecting life and those who have the view that it should be entirely the decision of the woman. I feel that I am in the middle.
I come to this debate with a great deal of experience. I have been elected at large across 560,000 people five times and have sat on the Metropolitan Toronto Council for 11 years. In that forum we had to debate this issue on a number of occasions. The area which I debated it that was the most sensitive was as the metro appointee to the Catholic Children's Aid Society. Therefore I have a very personal experience with some of the most heart-rending situations involving abortion that anyone could possibly have experienced.
Government Orders
I have a deep concern that the rights of women are respected on this issue. Yet, we as a society should be doing everything possible to prevent abortions. The act of abortion represents a failure and a tragedy.
I therefore have no problem with legislation in this field. It is important for Parliament to state its position, particularly when the rights of individuals can be so terribly affected.
There has been a very definite need for legislation since 1988. Things have not been fine. We have had two very newsworthy court cases with third party interventions. We have had the B.C. government attempt to legislate in this area, and there are several provinces that have attempted to restrict access. The opposition member's contention that everything has been just great since 1988 is simply not so.
If one looks at the statistics on abortions since 1988, the number of abortions has not risen. This statistic has been used to say that women have been acting responsibly. I think it also means that when there was a law they were also acting responsibly and there was no difficulty for women who wanted an abortion to get one in Canada, except for the problems of access in remote areas with which we have to deal in any event, law or no law.
Legislation in this area is not something that is negative. I do not think we are recriminalizing abortion. Abortion was not criminal before. Abortions that were outside the law were criminalized. Similarly this legislation makes abortions that are not in accordance with the law again criminalized.
The old law was not much of a problem. It was in for 17 years. The Morgentaler decision was around the issue of the abortion committee, which doctors also complained about. It was simply something that did provide a delaying effect, that when it was operating properly, as it was in most urban centres and major hospitals, there was really no real problem.
I do not think what we are talking about today is law. What we are talking about is whether or not there will be more court actions. I do not think that the law we are passing will affect the number of abortions in Canada. I do not think women have abortions for frivolous reasons. The fact that there has been no law and that there has been no change in the statistics indicates that.

May 23, 1990
Government Orders
What I am hoping will be prevented are court cases and the humiliation particular individuals suffered, as we saw so clearly last year. With this new law, if the medical association meets the challenge implicit in it, because the law makes the doctors really responsible for enforcing the ethics of their profession, and if the CMA responds by establishing procedures for doctors to follow and a standard consent form such as the one that Dr. Morgentaler uses which ensures that women are aware of alternatives to abortions, it will operate in an efficient and reasonable fashion.
The question of access is also improved by this law, because it establishes the right of a women to have an abortion in consultation with a doctor.
In addition, the medical innovations that are now occurring mean that in the future abortions will not be performed in hospitals. There is the new pill that has been approved in France and doctors are now talking about medical procedures in the abortion field being performed in their offices. This will mean that access will not be an issue in the future.
Let us turn to the rights of the foetus. According to this legislation, the foetus is entitled to consideration in balance with the rights of the woman to security of person. I do not think that the foetus has been ignored because doctors have been given that responsibility in accordance with their profession.
The Canadian Medical Association, according to their ethics, does not believe that it is professionally reasonable for a doctor to perform an abortion on a viable foetus, a viable foetus being one that weighs over 500 grams or is past 20 weeks of gestation. The CMA says that abortion should not be used as an alternative to contraception. Similarly, counselling services, family planning services and information on contraception must be readily available to all Canadians. It says that the patient should be provided with the option of full and immediate counselling services in the event of unwanted pregnancy. It talks about options for women.
This law makes it clearly the responsibility of doctors in the medical profession, in conjunction with women, to provide that kind of counselling and that kind of assurance to society that women who receive abortions are fully counselled as to their options and that prevention is also considered.
Those who would deny a woman the right to an abortion except if it threatens the life of the woman, her physical health in some dramatic way, do not, I think, appreciate the rights of women in this society. The Minister of Justice has already stated that she believes it would be unconstitutional to support those amendments.
I think those people also underestimate the seriousness of the psychological reasons that women have for abortions. In a pluralistic and democratic society such as ours, such a law would simply not be obeyed. One cannot force a law on society which affects people so individually or personally.
At the committee I asked the question how people could possibly think that such a law could be enforced in Canada if Ceausescu in Romania could not enforce such a law in the most severe dictatorship in the world.
Our society respects and cares about the rights of individuals. We have to deal with people with compassion. I think this law will ensure that, with the help and co-operation of the medical profession, that will be done.

Mr. Speaker, today I would like to talk about the amendments contained in Bill C-43, and especially in support of amendment no. 24 moved by one of my colleagues.
I feel somewhat uneasy reading this bill because I wonder if 85 per cent of the members of this House were women, would we vote for such a bill? I shall give you an example. As you know, Mr. Speaker, about 12 to 15 per cent of the members are now women. On examining this bill, I am struck by the lack of logic and plain common sense.
This bill came about as a result of the Morgentaler decision, as I am sure you recall, Mr. Speaker. After several Quebec courts had rendered decisions, a Quebec jury decided that Mr. Morgentaler had the right to perform therapeutic abortions. The people spoke. They said it was not a criminal matter. The decision to have an abortion is already hard enough; the public did not want to make it a crime. In the end, Dr. Morgentaler was found not guilty. It went to the Supreme Court, which confirmed and ratified the decisions of the other courts. Good! It is done.
May 23, 1990

But what happened is that two years ago, the federal government-that is us, Mr. Speaker, we are responsible-but especially the Conservative government said, "we will not leave that alone. No! We members of Parliament, we men know better. We will prepare a bill that will make everyone unhappy"-well, not everyone, but about 62 per cent of Canadians. And I understand that some Canadians are unhappy with the bill because they think it is against the unborn. There are others, especially in my party, who think this is not a step forward, a step toward a better understanding of the problem but a step backward. When the government says it wants to defend the interests of Quebec men and women-I trust the women of Quebec are included-I find it hard to understand how it can claim to protect those rights when we have before the House a bill that is so illogical in design and so unfair in its application, I would even go so far as to say, Mr. Speaker, a bill that is cruel and anti-women. How can I prove that? Easy. It means forcing a woman who has been raped to bear the child of the person who raped her! A young girl of 13 or 14 who was raped by her father would have to bear his child. Why? My colleagues will say, because they are convinced, which I do not doubt: because life is important. I ask you Mr. Speaker: whose life? The life-and one can debate whether life is there or not-of the foetus or the life of a young girl of 13 or 14? That is the problem.
I know we can talk about this for a long time. When does life start? At what point does the foetus become a human being?
The consequences of this legislation are disastrous. They are very negative for Canadian women. We have already seen it in Nova Scotia-in fact, that is why the Supreme Court dismissed the existing legislation- where women have lacked the same access as women in Ontario, British Columbia or elsewhere. In fact, this was pure discrimination.
The Canadian Medical Association has said, and these are experts, that if the bill is passed, doctors-the CMA speaks for the doctors-will limit access to abortion because they will be afraid of being put in jail.
I do not blame them. I realize that some hon. members here really want to do the right thing, and I understand
Government Orders
that, but by supporting this bill, they are doing the exact opposite.
Before I finish, Mr. Speaker, I just want to say that I am uncomfortable with this bill. I am comfortable with the fact that I am opposed to this legislation, but I am uncomfortable about the fact that a government has the arrogance to believe it has a monopoly on truth and to promote this kind of legislation which I think is unnecessary and, in the final instance, does not protect the interests of Quebecers and especially not the interest of the women of Quebec. That is why I am ashamed when I see this government which claims to defend the rights of men and women by proposing this kind of legislation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased once again to make a few comments on this very difficult and troubling subject for members of Parliament.
When this issue was before the House the last time I voted against the bill. Parliament at that time was being asked to give approval in principle to the bill and I said to Parliament at that time that I could not in good conscience give approval to something that I have always fought against in my life. I have fought for the protection of unborn children and I fought against the abortion law that was in place in Canada for many years.
Since I was being asked to give approval in principle, I said I could not do that. I decided at that time, having made the point, that I would consider the whole issue again. I listened very carefully to the arguments of individuals who said that this law was better than no law, that there were positive aspects to this law from both points of view, the pro-choice and the pro-life.
I looked at it not only for that reason but because of the profound respect that I have for other individuals in Parliament who are also struggling with this. One of the things that I have learned is that as difficult and important as these moral questions are, it is very difficult to come up with absolutes. Other members looking at the same set of circumstances can come to different conclusions as to what they should be doing and how they should be acting in this.

May 23, 1990
Government Orders
Having considered very carefully all the different sides of this issue, I have come to the conclusion that I will not be supporting the bill at report stage or third reading stage because it goes against a principle that I have fought for all my life, that is, my belief in the sacredness of human life. After having discussions with my colleagues, I realize there are good points in this, that it does recognize the value of human life, but I could not overcome my concerns with respect to the over-all implications of this bill.
I think there is a role for individuals who state their position very clearly and not move from that. Society itself, indeed the Supreme Court, recognizes, in cases of unborn children, the legitimate interest of society in the foetus. That is as it should be because it has always been my belief that the less articulate a particular interest is, the more likely it is that their interests will be compromised or not taken into consideration. I think there is a role for individuals such as myself, who believe as I do, to state very clearly their position.
I do not minimize the difficulties. I know the difficulties of the constitutional considerations in this area. As well, I do not know what words Parliament could come up with. I have no idea what could be put down on a piece of paper that would be acceptable to both sides of this issue. I do not know what those words would be. I give full credit to my colleagues and the leadership of my political party for putting together what I would not call a compromise but an accommodation of both sides. That is why in many ways it was very tempting for me to say that I could accept that, because I do not know what else could pass in Parliament.
However, I have other fears. I have fears about the removal of this issue from the public agenda. I have fears about how this bill will operate in practice. I could go on with those criticisms. I am sure that the criticisms of this bill have been very well articulated by members inside and outside of the House. It would be unfair for me to get into that when I know how difficult this has been.
For myself the way is clear, but that does not make it any less difficult for me. I will not be supporting the bill. I will also not be supporting, with the exception of one, the amendments. The so-called pro-life amendments do
not turn this into a pro-life bill. It would be hypocritical for me to get up this evening and support any one of 10 or 15 of these amendments and then ultimately find that the bill is unacceptable to me. It would be hypocritical to do that. I will not do that this evening and, with the exception of one, I will be voting against those amendments presently before the House.
One of the things I have learned about this is that there are no absolutes, and there is no way of coming to a conclusion about absolutes. People on all sides of this issue are sincere. I heard some speeches yesterday that I was somewhat disappointed to hear. People on either side of this issue were ascribing insincerity to the other side. I do not believe that. I believe that people on both sides of this issue are just as sincere about wanting to do the right thing.
As well, I heard at least one comment suggesting that the Prime Minister may be forcing government members to do something. I can say that those members do not know the Prime Minister of Canada. They are absolutely wrong in that conclusion. That is not the case. Members of this party are free to vote according to their conscience, which is one among many reasons why I am so proud to be a part of this government and this political party.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to participate in this debate and to express my views on a most sensitive human issue. It is a human issue. It affects all of us. To discuss the issue solely in the context of how it affects women is to ignore the fact that abortion affects men and children and, obviously, it affects the unborn.
I voted against the bill at second reading in the hope that it would be amended at committee stage. While a number of amendments were moved, the government has indicated that it is not willing to accept any of them. Therefore, I must make my position clear from the outset.
I believe that, since life begins at conception, life must be legally protected from the moment of conception. On that basis, I cannot support the bill in its present form because it does not effectively prohibit abortion and it does not protect the unborn. I am opposed to Bill C-43
May 23, 1990

in principle. I am opposed because this bill does nothing to solve the real dilemma of abortion.
I realize, however, that it is unproductive merely to criticize the government's proposals without making some alternative suggestions or general recommendations. That is why I would like also to address the need for a holistic approach to the abortion issue.
The main problem with this bill is that it fails to address fundamental issues. There is no mention of the rights of the foetus or the rights of women. Nowhere does it say that an unborn has a right to life and that this life should take precedence over a woman's expressed desire to "control her body". Nowhere in Bill C-43 is there an explicit recognition of the fact that a foetus is a human life. In fact, there is not even any mention of the foetus. How can a law on abortion make no mention of the existence of the foetus?
It seems clear to me that this bill is avoiding the fundamental issues. It dumps the problems onto the provinces, the doctors, and the courts.
What is the meaning of the term "health" in this bill? When Section 251 of the Criminal Code was struck down by the Supreme Court in the Morgentaler case of January, 1988, Chief Justice Dickson expressed concern that the term "health" was too vague. Bill C-43 does not rectify this problem. While there is attempt to respond to Chief Justice Dickson's concerns, I maintain that the qualifiers of "physical, mental and psychological" in Bill C-43 simply leave too many doors open. In fact, C-43 does not limit interpretation of "health" in any way. The definition could be extended to include anything and everything. One doctor can arrive at a conclusion that would make an abortion legal.
I support Motion No. 10 by which the word "health" would be eliminated. The bill in its present form will be susceptible to arbitrary limitations on application. It will be vulnerable to constitutional review on the basis of ambiguity. In fact, it seems clear that the issue may simply end up being passed on to the courts.
According to Professor Allan Hutchinson of Osgoode Hall Law School:
Anyone who thought the introduction of new legislation would end
the abortion debate will be disappointed. One chapter may be closing
but another is just beginning. Once the dramatic action in Parliament
Government Orders
ends, it will move down the hill to the more refined but no less heated
setting of the Supreme Court.
The courts, however, will not be alone in facing the abortion issue. With Bill C-43 the federal government is passing on an additional burden to the provinces. The federal government is responsible for criminal law and for guaranteeing that all Canadians receive the same level of insured medical services. However, if Bill C-43 is passed, the government will be abdicating these responsibilities because it will be the provinces which will ultimately have to decide such issues as whether abortions will be performed in their hospitals, whether abortion clinics will be licensed, and whether provincial health plans will cover the cost of abortions.
Finally, I would like to add that doctors will also be burdened by a great deal of decision-making concerning abortion. The responsibilities and the problems associated with these responsibilities will now be in the hands of the courts, the provinces, and the doctors. What an abdication of responsibility.
Effective solutions assume a good understanding of the problems. However, I firmly believe that in the case of abortion the real underlying problems have not been sufficiently dealt with or, in fact, understood. How can we provide solutions when we have not even properly identified the fundamental problem?
This is the crux of the matter. The fundamental problem is not the pregnancies themselves. It is the fact that they are unwanted. From this we must infer that the solution is not abortion on demand. Rather, the solution is to deal with the various forces that underlie the decision to have an abortion. We must examine why women have abortions. We must identify the pressures that push women to opt for abortions, and then it is our duty to do everything humanly possible to remove these pressures.
I would like to mention at this point that, contrary to the beliefs of many pro-choice advocates, being pro-life does not imply being anti-women. In fact, it is quite the contrary. We must encourage the development of support and counselling programs for women. We must recognize that many women, faced with the problem of an unwanted pregnancy, are lonely, afraid, deserted, usually poor and, perhaps worst of all, stigmatized by society. We must help these women. We must have programs that deal with the enormous social, economic, and psychological forces that push women to believe that

May 23, 1990
Government Orders
the only way out of a difficult situation is to abort their own children.
Abortion is a violent act. It is a violent act against unborn children and against women. It is time to understand why this violence occurs. It is time to stop this violence.
Bill C-43 does nothing to address the reasons why women abort. There is a desperate need for counselling and support programs. We must make facilities equally accessible to all women across the country. We must facilitate the adoption alternative. We must provide more child care facilities. We must provide child care bursaries for women with children who want to complete their education. After all, people are our most precious resource and we should invest in that resource.
There is no quick fix to the abortion problem. There is no easy solution. Bill C-43 is an attempt to have it both ways. It pays lip service to the pro-life movement by putting Bill C-43 in the Criminal Code. However, the content and the intent of the bill basically amount to abortion on demand. It will be a criminal offence to perform abortions unless any one doctor is prepared to say that the life or health of the mother is threatened. In essence, abortion is left to the discretion of the woman and her doctor.
I reiterate that I will not support this bill. I simply cannot support a bill that discriminates against the weakest and most defenceless members of our society.

Mr. Speaker, I have spoken many times on this issue. I am speaking now, of course, at report stage of Bill C-43 and against the motions nos. 4 to 19 which are very tough, restrictive and punitive amendments which would increase the criminal sanctions of Bill C-43. If the complete criminal prohibition of abortion fails, there are several amendments which would limit the definition of "health" as another tactic to try to restrict the choice of women.
It is significant that these extremely restrictive amendments are presented by anti-choice advocates. I am sorry to say this, but all members who presented these motions, and most of the members speaking to them, are men. The total impact of the abortion question concerns
women primarily and should be a private choice and decision of each woman.
I regret that some women members, who I know in their hearts prefer women to have a choice on the question of abortion, also will vote for Bill C-43. I can respect some of their feelings about this, but I note that there are none today who are speaking for the extremely restrictive and paternalistic Motions Nos. 4 to 19.
I would particularly like to commend the member from Toronto who spoke a few minutes ago for stressing prevention and the points she raised about the lack of reality of these motions in even achieving the goals that their movers sought in presenting them.
I would like to take a moment to pay tribute to the many men, and particularly our male colleagues in this caucus, who have supported the policy that abortion is not a criminal matter to be controlled by the state with severe criminal sanctions and limitations in criminal law. They recognize, as do the majority of Canadians, that this is an extremely personal matter that involves a very difficult personal decision for a woman who is faced with an unwanted, unplanned pregnancy. As such, it must be treated as a health matter with the decision to be made by the woman and her doctor.
We do not feel that criminal laws have any place in the question of reproductive and family planning matters. Experience over the past two years, since the Supreme Court decision was made in the Morgentaler case which rescinded the previous criminal laws, has shown that we do not need a new federal law. Abortions have not increased as a result of having open choice on this matter. Women have been treated with the respect and dignity they deserve, recognizing their right to decide themselves whether or not they are ready to have a child.
The present situation, where we have no abortion law, is much more respectful of doctors and medical associations generally. Doctors and medical associations have established regulations and health standards that are the only kinds of controls needed.
If a woman decides not to continue a pregnancy, whether it is because she is alone without support, is in an abusive relationship, is a young girl with no means of support to raise a family, or wants to wait and plan a family later, whatever the reason-and there are many, many complex reasons-this is a safe medical procedure performed by a physician who does not feel intimidated
May 23, 1990

or subject to criminal sanctions. There is no criminal law imposed on the woman or the doctor. That is one of the reasons we object to the bill. The major problem for women today is the lack of access, particularly in the Atlantic region and rural and remote areas. That is where we should focus our action.
The series of amendments, numbered 4 to 19, being debated this afternoon are restrictive, cruel and undemocratic, based on outdated, patriarchal views of women, the fact that women must be controlled by the state- and the state is usually a patriarchal institution-they cannot be trusted and must be controlled and punished with tough criminal sanctions. That is what these particular amendments are saying to Canadian women and to Canadians generally.
It is sickening to know that there are people in Canada, and members in this House, who support these resolutions, who want to impose the kind of inhumane policies that we saw in Romania where women were forced to have babies and these babies were neglected and abused. A whole generation is almost destroyed and disturbed and society as a whole has suffered greatly.
Do we really want this kind of authoritative dictatorship in Canada? Most Canadians do not. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, and members of the House, that that is what these amendments mean to many women. These amendments and their movers show that they have no empathy for the condition of women who face very difficult decisions and no respect for the rights of women to make their own choices as to whether or not now is the time to have a family.
I would like to refer to the main motions to which I object. First, Motions Nos. 4 and 22, if passed, would increase the criminal penalty from two to 20 years, a 20-year imprisonment for doctors who perform abortions. Doctors perform abortions now because they see it as a health measure and a necessity in individual cases. This is not only completely intolerable for doctors but would also increase criminal penalties for women.
Motion No. 5 states that abortions will be performed only by a medical practitioner. The medical associations have objected to this and have agreed that in certain situations there could be medical procedures under the direction of a medical practitioner. We know that this is directed to women who would have self-induced abortions. I wonder what some of the proponents of these
Government Orders
amendments would do about morning-after pills which is a form of abortion. What are they going to do about monitoring that, I wonder. There are no beneficial effects to any of these amendments, only negative ones.
For example, Motion No. 10 proposes that the only abortions that would be legal would be those performed in order to save the life of a woman. Other abortions performed for the woman's health would be illegal. Surely, that does not make sense. It certainly does not make sense to me.
Another amendment would force a woman by threat of criminal sanction to carry a foetus to term unless she meets certain criteria. This is a profound interference with a woman's body and thus, an infringement on the security of the person. This is what Chief Justice Dickson said about the old law and would certainly say the same about this amendment.
Motion No. 13 makes a bad bill worse. Health is not the issue. Unwanted pregnancy is the issue. Motion No. 14 is another one that would strike out the definition of health.
Motions Nos. 16, 17A and 17B are ones I am very interested in because we have had at least two doctors in this House who have spoken about the question of health. They seem to disregard completely the UN definition of health, and also, what I understand to be psychosomatic medicine which relates to the psychological and physical aspects of health. It is very difficult, if you have a whole approach to medicine, to separate these.
Certainly, I wonder if a woman under extreme stress and anxiety is a healthy woman. I do not think so, and I do not think she would really be in a position to be a healthy mother. The rationale about health as a reason is particularly offensive.
Motion No. 19 refers to scientific knowledge. I would think that, surely, physicians have access to scientific knowledge now. This seems to be an insult to the medical profession.
In summary, there are many reasons why I and my party object to these resolutions and will vote against them. They criminalize abortion in the extreme and are not a deterrent, because women will still seek out back street abortions or self-induced abortions. They will be victims of quacks and butchers as the women in Romania

May 23, 1990
Government Orders
were. It was the experience in Italy when abortion was very restricted.
