speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, far be it from me to quarrel with you or the Whip.
I am going to be very brief today, because my position on this issue was dealt with at some length in the 1988 debate on the motions that were before the House at that time. The philosophical approach that I had was outlined at that time but I would like to make a few comments on the process, the amendments and on the bill itself, to illustrate the tremendous dichotomy of views that one encounters in dealing with this issue.
First, with reference to process, I am pleased that I am afforded the opportunity as a member of Parliament on the government side to have a free vote in this instance. In many ways, parliamentary secretaries are members of the government and are regarded as such within our system. I appreciate having the opportunity to vote according to my conscience on what I think is a very fundamental issue.
I listened with great interest to the hon. member for Vancouver East and her comments about the amendments. I believe it is her position that her party is for choice, but her party does not seem to have a choice available to its individual members on this issue.
With reference to the amendments themselves, I believe that all those who were involved with the process of putting forward amendments and considering the possibility of amendments while the bill was in committee and those who have put them on the Order Paper for consideration here today have borne in mind a number of criteria. The first is to do that which is proper and right. The second is to do that which is politically
achievable and the third is to do that which will meet the test of the Supreme Court of Canada.
It is my considered opinion that a number of the amendments before us-I refer to Motions Nos. 12, 13, and 17B, in particular, but not excluding the others-will stand a court test. I concede that there is opinion on both sides of the issue, but I have seen opinions I respect from three very substantial and distinguished sources that these amendments would stand a court test.
I want to relate what happened one Friday afternoon in February when I was seeing constituents, as we all do, in my riding office. I had had a rather testy exchange of correspondence with a constituent who represented a significant interest group, not only within the constituency but also nationally.
This constituent had written to me taking me to task for what she perceived to be, with some accuracy, my position on this issue. She suggested that "no one group", as she put it, "had the right to impose its view on others within a pluralistic society".
I met with this woman, had lunch with her and tried to come to grips with this and other issues which she had raised in her correspondence with me. I stressed to her my belief that if there is not an ethical and moral basis for our law, then we are steering by the bow, rather than by the tiller. In this issue we tend to fall into the whirlpool of losing respect for life itself.
I listened with care to the member for Vancouver East, and I know it will sound patronizing to her ears and to the ears of a number of my colleagues in this House, but I do not think the issue is controlling women when we address this bill. The issue is respect for life. That is why I see a series of amendments on the Order Paper.
On that same day, I returned to my constituency office and met with an obstetrician who I thought was of the Catholic faith, because of his well-known position on the abortion issue. He was, of course, opposed to abortion but I learned that he was a Muslim. I had not known that, prior to meeting with him. He gave me his view and, as he left my office, a young woman came in to see me. Neither the man who was leaving nor the young woman
May 23, 1990

who was coming in, knew that the other would be there. They were father and daughter.
The daughter had organized a pro-life group on the campus of the University of Alberta. She said it was uphill because it was not the most popular cause on a campus, but she had recruited 75 members for that group and was hoping to have a national meeting of like-minded groups from campuses across the country.
I asked her what message she conveyed to young women in particular, but also to young men who joined her group as well. I asked what she advocated they do in our society and what kind of code of behaviour she advocated. She said: "fun within the framework of chastity". Those words may seem absurd in today's society and in fact the woman with whom I had lunch said: "Let's face it. The fact of the matter is that the vast bulk of teenagers and young people today are having sex and so we have to face that reality."
The point I am making is that there is an issue of responsibility here, not just responsibility for women but also for men to endeavour to control their activity and, if they are not able to do so, to take reasonable precautions to minimize the consequences.
Now we come to the obvious, the amendments themselves. We face the possibility of none of the amendments succeeding tonight, and which way do we go on the bill itself when the vote comes up next Tuesday, May 29.
There are many people who know my position on the issue who are urging me to vote against the bill. They are saying that it is better to have no bill than to have a flawed bill. Frankly, I do not know how I am going to vote if the amendments do not succeed. I hope some of the amendments do succeed.
If the goal is as I have suggested, to respect life and to spare lives, which is the lesser evil: to have no bill, or to have the bill that is before us? When one deals with the issue of lesser evil-a much abused term, by the way, Mr. Speaker-one must clearly identify that there are no alternatives before one. Clearly in this case there are not if the amendments do not succeed. One must also analyze whether the options have components of evil or lack of good in them. Both clearly do.
Government Orders
If, on the other hand, the goal is to find a bridgehead on which the principle of respect for life can be nurtured and encouraged, to await the day when through education and a change of heart this country will come to a different attitude on the issue of abortion without in one slightest way demeaning the rights of women and in fact enhancing the rights of women, and can define a parallel right of the foetus or the unborn individual, then that is a goal to be pursued.
I will be listening with great care to the debate not only today but tomorrow. I have consulted with my constituents. I have written all those who have been in correspondence with me on the issue and I have said, among other things:
-if the Bill emerges from Report Stage unamended, is it better to vote for it, imperfect as it is, or against it, which would leave us with no abortion law whatsoever for the foreseeable future?
My judgement at this point is that the Bill would discourage some doctors who perform some abortions from continuing to do so. I am not at all sure that it would save substantial numbers of unborn lives. But it would make a statement that performing abortions is a breach of the Criminal Code (except in certain very broad circumstances).
That is the issue before us, an issue from my point of view of deciding between lesser evils. I will be praying for guidance, but I will also be listening to my colleagues for guidance because there is a good body of wisdom in this House.

Mr. Speaker, first of all, if men were able to become pregnant, would we be debating this bill? I rather think not. That is a question I would like to put because I, as a man, do not have a clue what it is like to be pregnant. I think we, as men, should admit that we are rather unqualified to judge the issue of what to do about pregnancy.
I do not condone abortion as birth control. I doubt that very many people do, regardless of whether they are pro-life, anti-abortion or pro-choice. I make the mistake of saying pro-life because I think that is the name given to people who call themselves pro-lifers. It is a misnomer, a mistaken label, because I do not think anyone has a monopoly on caring about life. I care about life just as much as anyone else. I do not think that is debatable. If you are pro-choice it does not mean that you do not care about life.

May 23, 1990
Government Orders
I would like to state something that should be understood by some people here in the House. I think there is some hypocrisy in attitudes of non-aboriginal people. In the Inuit culture there is no such thing as an unwanted child. We have a custom called custom adoption. I am adopted. I have five adopted children. That is not because these children were not wanted, but because I had talked to whoever had the children and we decided we could take care of the child better than the mother, or maybe because we did not have children of our own.
I would like to elaborate on this. When I say some of us are pro-choice, I talk about people in general. When I talk about Inuit, you will find that most Inuit are anti-abortion but unlike some people down here who are anti-abortion, Inuit do not just pay lip service to the issue of abortion or anti-abortion. They practise what they preach. If they are against abortion, it is because they are prepared to take care of the children whether they be of single mothers or relatives. They are prepared to adopt and again, there is no stigma in adoption. When I was adopted I knew exactly who my natural parents were as well as my adopted parents, and so do my five adopted children. They know exactly who their natural parents are or who their natural parent is, in some cases. When I say they practise what they preach, that is exactly what it is.
In the Eastern Arctic there are no receiving homes for unwanted children. That is because all children are adopted. I would like to ask-and again, I do not condone abortion as birth control-those people who want to either restrict or even tighten the bill, how many are taking care of unwanted children that they got because they cared enough, and did not condone abortion. I am sure there are some, as the hon. member across just raised his hand, but I think the question is how many of those people who demonstrate in the streets against abortion, whether it be here, in Toronto or Vancouver, have children that they took because they cared enough about homeless children. I think that many of them would be hard pressed to admit that they have any.
I think that when women are pro-choice, it does not mean that they take abortion lightly. I think when women decide to have an abortion, it is not just one day deciding: "Well, I am going to get pregnant and I am
going to have an abortion." I do not think it is that simple. I think when women make the decision to have an abortion, it is an agonizing and very painful decision. I find it very difficult to believe that those decisions are made lightly. How can you inflict punishment on a person who, after very agonizing, painful thinking, has decided to have an abortion? How can you inflict criminal charges against that person?
If we were in an ideal world, we would not have abortion. However, the fact remains that there are women who are going to continue to have abortions and, frankly, that is probably the way life is at this point.
I would like to state that I am going to be voting against this bill because it criminalizes women when the decision to have an abortion is a very, very personal one.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak at report stage of Bill C-43,1 want to make it very clear at the outset that I will be voting against Bill C-43 on third reading. At report stage I will oppose all of the proposed amendments except for Motion No. 24, which stands in the name of the hon. member for New Westminster-Burnaby.
In an issue which touches personal conscience such as this one does, I have the greatest of respect for the feelings and opinions of all members which they hold very deeply.
Abortion has been an issue that has been very difficult for some people more than others. I suspect particularly some of them on the government side feel themselves torn by conflicting loyalties. All of us have those at times, but I think it probably bears more so on some members of the cabinet. As an individual who shares accommodation with some of those members, I must say that I appreciate the agony I am sure that they are going through.
In the contemporary lexicon of the abortion debate, I am unequivocally pro-choice and make no apology for it. I hold this view not because it is the position of my party. In fact I have argued on numerous occasions that it is in my opinion not the sort of issue which should be enshrined as a party issue or policy, because like religion or creed it is more properly a matter of individual conscience, personal philosophy and individual choice.
May 23, 1990

This has caused some difficulty for some members of my party, not here in the House of Commons but in the constituency and elsewhere, who during election campaigns have been active members of Pentecostal assemblies and do not hold a pro-choice point of view. Regardless of that, because we agree on a multitude of issues we have actively campaigned for our party and for myself when I have unequivocally taken a pro-choice point of view. I feel the discomfort that I know that they have felt on occasion.
Intolerance is not something that is exclusive to any particular political philosophy or creed. We all have our problems at times. It is difficult in the heat of debate to accord to all others the rights and full respect that we demand for ourselves.
I am pro-choice because I believe firmly that only the individual most closely affected, the woman, the potential mother, has the right ultimately to determine whether or not a pregnancy should be brought to term. In the final analysis she and she alone has the right to determine whether she will bear a child and when: not me, not us, not the police, not the courts, and not the criminal law.
Nothing could be more abhorrent or inappropriate than for the state to impose values on people regarding such an intensively personal issue as whether or not someone shall bear children. That is a woman's right. Women have shown throughout history, often at great cost to themselves, that they will exercise the right to choose regardless of risk or law, whether the law is religious, civil or criminal.
Rights exist not because we grant them, not because the law grants rights or society grants rights. Rights exist not because we grant them, not because the law grants rights, or society grants rights. Rights exist because people claim them and exercise them, often at great cost to themselves. When a large number of individuals have consistently shown that in order to exercise what they believe to be their fundamental rights they have to place themselves at risk, it does not behove us to impose our values by using the state or the law to try to force them to do otherwise.
That is bad law. It is bad law in this case. It is bad law in labour relations. It is bad law in a whole host of other areas. All that kind of action means-and regardless of
Government Orders
our point of view on this issue we all know it-is that women who claim this fundamental right to choose will continue to do so regardless of the penalties and regardless of the risk to themselves. If we pass such a law, it will simply bring the law and the institutions which pass and enforce those laws into contempt. We do not need any more of that than we already have in this day and age.
Do we really want to force women or large numbers of women to risk their lives as they have done before or be branded as criminals or sent to jail for exercising what they understandably regard as their right to choose whether or not to give birth? I do not want that, and I will not be a party to imposing my values on them.
With regard to values I said earlier that I have always resisted those people-whether they are on the right, on the left, or in the centre, no party is excluded-who from time to time want to use the law to impose their personal values or their moral judgments upon others or upon society. That is not my role, and I do not believe it should be our role.
I would like to make a few personal comments on the matter of language. A lot of very charged language has been used in this debate back and forth across the country. We have heard the phrase unborn children or unborn babies being used instead of the term fertilized eggs or foetuses or whatever.
I am not a religious person in the classical sense, but I value life every bit as much as someone who believes that all life has been created by a divine being. I believe that all life exists as a result of an infinitesimal number of accidents of fate over an infinitesimal number of years, trillions of years, beyond reckoning. I think that perhaps I regard it even more preciously because I do not believe that that combination of circumstances could ever likely occur again. I am not one who believes that there is a creator that is going to give us a second chance some day if we do not manage right now. I do not question the importance that others put on life, but I put just as much importance on it.
The whole debate of when life begins is a very moot point. I have no great certainty as to that point. I cannot accept the view of others who say: "Bang, this is when it starts." Life is an ongoing process. Life exists in a tree. It exists in an ant. It exists in the foetus. It exists in an individual human being who acts independently. I also

May 23, 1990
Government Orders
believe in social order, and I know we sometimes have to reach compromises on that.
In conclusion I want to say as a personal note that my wife and I have three children and have been married almost 30 years. I have a daughter. If as a teenager she were to have come to me and asked my counsel-this would have been a few years ago-because through an act of neglect or passion she found herself to be pregnant, probably in those circumstances I would have suggested that her life might be better and that she would have a better chance to have a happy life and a happy family in the future if she did have an abortion. There is no way that I would impose that on her. I would be one of the sources of counsel that she would seek, but it would be her decision. I would also tell her that regardless of what decision she took I would stand by her. As a society we need to provide nurturing, to provide the means for people to be capable of making that independent judgment, and not to impose our values or criminal sanctions on them for doing what comes naturally, that is to decide for themselves whether or not they shall bear children.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to participate in the debate this afternoon. This is actually the last opportunity that I will have to speak prior to the very crucial votes that will take place later today.
Initially, after proposing the amendments that I had to offer, I had not intended on speaking again prior to the vote that will take place tonight. I listened attentively yesterday and today to the remarks of my colleagues on both sides of the House, members of parliament, some who agree with me and some who profoundly disagree. Of course I believe all of them feel very strongly about their particular point of view and most-and I say "most"-are respectful of the point of view of others.
It is with sadness that I use the word "most" rather than the word "all" for the following reasons: a few members have seen fit during this debate to state that I was unqualified to speak on this issue because I am a man. If I were to say that the members in question who made those remarks cannot speak of building bridges because they are women, I would be condemned and
rightfully so. Of course I never have, nor do I intend to. All members representing constituents in this House are equal and worthy regardless of sex, age, gender, colour or otherwise. It is unfortunate that some people saw fit to utilize that argument. I suppose it only weakens the other strong arguments that they may have had.
However, that sadness having been stated, perhaps we should speak of the issue at hand rather than allow myself to stoop to the level that they have chosen to utilize to make their respective points in the House of Commons. Instead I would like to take this last opportunity to urge colleagues to vote for a number of the amendments offered to us.
The last colleague who spoke did raise a number of interesting points. I do not agree with his point of view, but I do think he expressed it quite well. He said, I believe, that he did not know whether life started at conception. I suppose I agree with his proposition there too. I do not know either. Unless someone proves otherwise, what else am I to conclude? If we know that human life is there at birth, it must have been achieved some time before birth. If no one indicates to me at which time before birth it occurs, then I am to assume that it was there from the beginning unless proven otherwise. That, I believe, is the only reasonable conclusion to arrive at. I am still awaiting anyone who challenges that proposition to indicate specifically at what time it is they feel my proposition is wrong. Mr. Speaker, whenever we are collectively and individually as a society afraid of an issue, I suppose we resort to words that tend to hide the facts that we are afraid of. A child born is obviously a child; a child unborn is a foetus-which means a young one in Latin-so my colleagues who are medical doctors tell me. Why do we use Latin, versus English or French, other than to specifically avoid using words that are uncomfortable to us? But we seem to use these words quite comfortably when they suit our individual purposes.
I have here a cover from a package of cigarettes which was given to me by another colleague, because I do not smoke. On this cover of the package of cigarettes, it says: "Smoking during pregnancy can harm the baby". It does not harm the "foetus"; it does not harm the "embryo"; it does not harm anything else. But it harms the "baby" during pregnancy.
May 23, 1990

Other colleagues have gone to great pains to tell us that it is not a baby, it is a foetus. I suppose those colleagues will want to make the cigarette manufacturers aware of the fact that they have this horrible mistake, according to them, on the jacket of this cigarette box.
I have an article here from the Canadian Press which refers to an incident which happened in Kingston, Ontario. A woman had been prescribed the wrong medicine which could result in her unborn child dying prior to birth. In other words, it could have resulted in an abortion. I quote from the article:
"At night I have dreams about what might happen to my child,''said
Mrs. Debney, 23. "We still have another five months to go before we
know what happens to the baby."
As I said in my speech yesterday, what we have is a situation where if we seem to want the child to be born, there is no hesitation in calling the child a baby. If we do not want the child, then it becomes the foetus. As I indicated yesterday, the child is not a child by virtue of the fact that we want it or not; the child is a child because that is what the child is, and that is the end of it.
To that extent I invite colleagues to reflect upon that when they are called upon later today to vote on the various amendments, particularly Motion No. 10, because it is that amendment which would change the bill in such a way as to give value to human life. I suppose other amendments will do so, but I believe to a lesser degree.
In conclusion, I just want to inform the House of how I intend to vote later today.

Mr. Speaker, I intend to support Motions Nos. 4, 5,10, 12, 13, 14, 16, 17A and B,-although in the case of 17A, this Motion may have very little impact-Motion No. 19 and Motion No. 22. I intend to vote against Motion No. 24. Of course, I repeat what I said several days ago: If Motion No. 10 is not passed, I will have to vote against this bill on third reading.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, I urge all hon. members to examine their consciences thoroughly, whether they agree with me or not, and to vote according to their conscience. I know that will be the case with our hon. members across the way, because there is no discipline in
Government Orders
their caucus, any more than there is in mine. Members are free to vote any way they want.
I hope all members will have that choice. And since we are talking about free choice, I think we should all have the free choice to vote for protecting human life.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak today to Bill C-43, an act respecting abortion.
When the Prime Minister indicated that his government would bring forward a bill on abortion during this session of Parliament, there was a collective sigh of relief across the country. That relief, however, was quickly shattered with the introduction of this bill. Bill C-43 completely fails to address the painful issue that is troubling this country's conscience.
I realize this is not a decision to be made lightly. I intend to vote against the bill in its present form. I believe this bill is a bad piece of legislation. Many of my constituents from the riding of Scarborough-Agincourt believe as I do, that human life begins at conception and must be protected by law at all stages of development.
Once we come to the unavoidable conclusion that the foetus is a human being, we must then come to the conclusion that this person must be given full protection of the law as would be given to any child in Canada today.
It is absolutely deplorable that anyone can say that a procedure which kills one human being for the convenience of another is a medical procedure. In simple terms, abortion is the killing of a human being and cannot be accepted. If we do not believe in life, then what can we believe in? Where is the value system? If we do not ensure that abortions are performed only to save the mother's life, then our society will be condoning abortion on demand.
I did not vote for Bill C-43 on second reading. Though I was disappointed that the bill reached committee stage, I hoped we would see some substantial amendments after the legislative committee had an opportunity to thoroughly examine the bill clause by clause. This was obviously not the case. I had hoped for an entirely different bill from the one we see before us today.

May 23, 1990
Government Orders
The abortion issue has not been rectified. The bill still does not recognize the fundamental value and dignity of each human being and the worth of each human life. I ask members of the House to consider the lives of unborn children above all else.
The only amendment that I can in conscience support is the one put forward by my colleague from Glengarry- Prescott-Russell which removes the word "health" from the bill. This would end any dubious claims of mental, emotional, fiscal or other reasons of so-called health which could be encompassed by such a broad definition.
This bill was flawed from the outset, and I dare say would not stand up constitutionally in a court of law. Therefore, it should not be before us at this time. It is obvious that the government, in choosing to put forward this bill at this particular time, decided it does not wish to deal with the real matter at hand, which is that of foetal rights.
The passage of this bill will lay open the door to medical experimentation upon the pre-born and would also leave open the question of usage of foetal tissue for dubious medical purposes.
I would also like to express my disappointment in the government's decision not to allow the free vote on this bill as was promised and expected.
I read in the paper today that some of my colleagues on the other side, members of cabinet, who are pro-life supporters will vote in favour of the bill. That saddens me. The constraints placed upon cabinet ministers to support this abortion bill is unconscionable.
I call upon all my colleagues in the House to give thought to why we are not addressing the real issues here today and to defeat this bill so that a comprehensive bill that looks at all the issues of foetal rights could be brought forward, or failing that, the rights of the unborn be placed where they rightfully belong, in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms of Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is not a compromise bill. It is a bill to recriminalize abortion. These are not compromise amendments. In fact, most of them are extreme, punitive and repugnant to women.
The Minister of Justice claims that the federal government must occupy the field on abortion. The field has not been occupied for two years, yet the numbers of abortions in Canada have not increased and the field does not appear to need to be occupied.
The minister says that this bill provides a delicate balance between both sides of the issue. I think not. This bill has failed on both sides of the question and there is no real balance at all. The women of Canada do not believe that this bill is giving us balance on both sides of the question.
The minister says that this bill respects constitutional guarantees. The women of Canada do not believe this bill respects constitutional guarantees, and most of the amendments fly in the face of constitutional guarantees. This bill is not an accommodation of common ground, as the minister says, that respects individual rights and freedoms. The women of Canada do not believe that it is the accommodation of common ground.
As a woman, I have been offended by many of the speeches in this House on the amendments to this bill, and indeed, by many of the amendments that have been put forward. The amendments to this bill suggest that women cannot be trusted. If men could be trusted to take their share of responsibility for birth control, we would not be having the debate on these amendments in this House today.
Let me deal specifically with the amendments. Motions Nos. 4 and 22 are amendments that, if passed, would increase the criminal penalty for doctors who perform abortions from two to 20 years. These amendments also have the side effect of increasing criminal penalties for women who have abortions. Obviously, these are not amendments that most Canadians, men or women, can subscribe to.
Motion No. 5 proposes that a legal abortion can only be performed by a medical practitioner. Essentially, this amendment imposes the threat of a two-year jail term and criminal record for a woman who induces her own abortion. If a woman is desperate enough to self-induce an abortion, she needs medical help and access to safe, affordable medical services. She does not need to be thrown in jail. Women self-induce an abortion only when they cannot get safe medical abortions or if the procedure is too costly.
May 23, 1990

Having a criminal penalty hanging over women's heads is not a deterrent, as we can see from the numbers of self-induced abortions that occurred when abortion was completely illegal. It is still illegal in some countries.
Motion No. 10, the motion that the member who just spoke said that he would support particularly, if passed, would mean that the only legal abortions would be those performed in order to save the life of the woman. Even abortions performed for the woman's health would be illegal. This is the most severe and cruel of all of the amendments associated with high maternal mortality rates. It is also the most controlling of women's bodies. Essentially, it is the former Romanian abortion law. There are only a few countries in the world left that still have this type of law.
While I am on the subject of the speech by that hon. member, I would like to point that he took exception to the fact that somebody in the debate disqualified him because he was a man. He tried to use the analogy of building a bridge. The ability to bear children and the consequences of that ability are quite different from the ability to build a bridge. Unfortunately, it is that kind of analogy that I think would disqualify him from speaking with any kind of authority on the question of abortion.
Motion No. 12 adds that in order for an abortion to be legal, a woman's life or health must be seriously endangered. This is an unconstitutional amendment. It contradicts the opinion expressed by Chief Justice Brian Dickson of the Supreme Court of Canada. In the Morgentaler case that struck down the old abortion law, he said that forcing a women by threat of criminal sanction to carry a foetus to term unless she meets certain criteria unrelated to her own priorities and aspirations is a profound interference with a woman's body and thus an infringement of the security of the person.
Motion No. 13 would change the bill to state that an abortion should be legal only if there is no other medical treatment available to alleviate the health risk to the woman. This amendment plays upon the government's own wording that the only legal abortions are those performed for the woman's health. It takes the govern-
Government Orders
ment's bad bill and makes it worse. Health is not the issue-unwanted pregnancy is.
Motion No. 14 would strike out the definition of health in the bill which states:
"health" includes, for greater certainty, physical, mental and
psychological health;
Medical professionals who appeared before the legislative committee complained that the health criteria in the bill were already too vaguely defined. This motion only exacerbates that.
Motions Nos. 16, 17A and 17B all change the definition of health in the bill to exclude psychological health considerations.
Motion No. 19 is a bizarre amendment. It would change the bill by clarifying medical opinions of whether or not to grant abortions should be developed, not only according to generally accepted medical standards as expressed in the bill, but also by considering the solid body of scientific knowledge.
Motion No. 20 would make the IUD and the morning-after pill illegal. I do not think that this amendment even requires further debate.
Motion No. 24, which would strike out the entire bill, would leave only one sentence which would state that Sections 287 and 288 of the Criminal Code are repealed. This motion in fact is the motion that addresses the inequities of the government's bill. This is the motion that most of my colleagues, and most people who want to reflect the needs of Canadian women, will support when we vote tonight.
In closing, I say that it is very sad that what the government has said about a woman's rights-her right to be a full participant in Canadian society-tells Canadian women where they stand with the government. It is this: "You are free and you can fully participate, as long as you understand that we do not trust your ability to make correct choices".

Mr. Speaker, I feel very privileged and honoured to be able to participate in debate a second time on Bill C-43, this time at report stage.
In my previous vocation as an educator I taught students, and I taught teachers to teach students, certain values in life. Some of those values were based on the three Rs. Those three Rs were not reading, 'ritin' and arithmetic. The three Rs were respect, respect, and

May 23, 1990
Government Orders
respect-respect for authority, respect for property, and respect for others.
If all Canadians today had a greater respect for the authority of the federal government, then maybe we would not be in the mess we are in. If all Canadians had a greater respect for property, then maybe our environment would not be in such jeopardy. If all Canadians had respect for others, then maybe we would not have this heated debate over whether we should allow a foetus to live or not.
I have carried these values into politics. Because I have this deep respect for others, which means respect for life, I cannot support Bill C-43 as it stands. To me, life begins at conception. Unless someone proves otherwise, I have to go on that belief.
I want to congratulate all those speakers who have debated this bill at second reading and report stage for the seriousness with which they have dealt with this problem. I want to congratulate those who promoted the pro-choice ideology, and the ones who promoted the pro-life ideology. I am convinced that both sides spoke very sincerely. They believe in what they told us. They are going to vote according to what they believe in. I am pleased that at least the two major parties are allowing us to vote according to our conscience.
I am a little disappointed in the New Democratic Party because I thought that it was the party which respects individual thoughts and ideas. I appeal to its members that on this issue they make an exception. Rather than vote as a party, let the members vote according to their conscience. In speaking to some members of the New Democratic Party, I know that their feelings are pro-life feelings also. That is an appeal to the New Democratic Party.
I also appeal to the people who believe in the prochoice ideology. We have heard the statements: "It's my body. I will decide what I want to do with it", et cetera. That argument breaks down because, in that free choice, two lives are at stake. If the choice was made just for one life, okay, I could maybe accept it, but the decision made affects two human beings. As a result of that, I cannot accept it.
Judgments of jurisprudence have been made to recognize clearly that the foetus is a human being. If a woman who is pregnant gets killed in a car accident, courts have
ruled that two people are killed. The case is treated with greater seriousness and gravity. Also, if a human being who was a foetus during the course of an accident survives, then he or she can sue the person causing the accident. Legislators and judges in the past must have recognized that the foetus is a human being.
The member for Vancouver East called the amendments that we brought in punitive and paternalistic. I would ask her to look at the amendments brought in by the members for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell and Winnipeg North, as well as the amendment of the member for Markham-Whitchurch-Stouffville. These amendments would strengthen Bill C-43 to protect the lives of the unborn. If these amendments were accepted, then I might be able to vote in favour of the bill.
I took a very extensive poll in my riding of Parkdale- High Park. People supporting both ideologies, the prolife ideology and the pro-choice ideology, have urged me to vote against this bill. At this point I do not think we know the outcome of Bill C-43. In talking to members individually, they are also going to look at which amendments will be accepted and which ones will not.
But whichever way the vote goes, I would like to recommend through you, Mr. Speaker, that the government introduce a national education program on this issue. The government can call it the national education program on life, or whatever title it wants, but there should be a national program funded by the federal government, supervised by the Department of National Health and Welfare.
The curriculum for this program would have to be written with input from the provinces, since the provinces have jurisdiction over education; from people who are supporting the pro-life ideology; from the prochoice people; from the medical profession; and from religious groups. By having a curriculum taught in all schools across the country, hopefully fewer young teenagers would get pregnant and have to make that very serious decision. In many cases, whichever decision is made, there are very deep-rooted emotional problems that follow.
In closing, I again appeal to the government to bring in a national education program on this issue, whichever way the vote goes.
May 23, 1990

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to voice my concerns regarding Bill C-43 as the member of Parliament for Beaver River, but I also want to voice the concerns of my constituents. Certainly, I have a personal feeling about this issue, but I am responsible for my constituents.
I want to speak today obviously as a woman, but I believe firmly that this is not just a woman's issue. It certainly is a family issue and an issue that faces all of us as a society.
My party calls for a candidate to let constituents know how he or she feels about the abortion issue. Then, if there is a consensus in the riding, the member of Parliament must vote according to the collective wishes of the constituents as determined by a referendum, such as a questionnaire, or at public meetings that determine whether or not there is a clear consensus. If there is no clear consensus, then the member of Parliament must vote according to his or her conscience and, of course, they have let that be publicly known while campaigning.
This approach certainly is somewhat different than we have traditionally seen from many members of Parliament. ffistory shows that MPs often have gone directly against the wishes of the majority of their constituent's wishes and said that they want to go for their conscience alone and vote on behalf of that. Unfortunately, we know that it is not just a member's conscience that got them elected. They had only one vote to cast on election day. They were voted in by many electors to whom they are responsible. A member of Parliament gets only one vote in the Elouse of Commons and that is not a personal vote, necessarily, but one vote on behalf of their entire riding.
I want to make it publicly known, and I have told my constituents in Beaver River, that I am pro-life. I am not ashamed of those views. In fact, it makes me proud to be able to say that I believe in the sanctity of life from the moment of conception. Those who deny that life begins at conception, deny the fundamental issue of life itself. A life cannot begin just at birth. If there had not been union nine months before, obviously there would be no live birth.
If we tiy to determine at what point life occurred, or whether or not an embryo a foetus is a life, then we miss the point of life itself. A human life begins at the
Government Orders
moment of conception, not before and not after. Whether we like it or not, science dictates, not semantics.
I conducted the closest thing that I could to a referendum in my riding. The results were very interesting. The totals were 60 per cent to 40 per cent pro-life, with people in those categories saying that they could make exceptions. Exceptions could be made in cases of rape, incest, and when the life of the woman is in danger.
I will be voting that way at third reading, unless Motion No. 10 specifically goes through tonight at report stage.
Regardless of the fact that everyone has different views, whether pro-life or pro-choice, it seemed to me that the people in my riding felt very serious frustration and misgivings about this particular bill.
In fact, Bill C-43 unfortunately satisfies neither end of the spectrum. Those at the pro-life end of the spectrum say that this bill does nothing more than give abortion on demand, and they are very, very concerned about the idea of psychological health as is stated in Bill C-43. Those at the pro-choice end of the spectrum are upset about Bill C-43 because, first, it goes back into the Criminal Code and they do not want that and, second, there is no access for healthy women to have abortions. No matter at what end of the spectrum people are, they are concerned about this bill.
I do believe that although I am pro-life and am not ashamed to admit that, as I said earlier, people say: "We are pro-choice and that is the way it is". I do believe that there is room for pro-choice. That choice rests with the individual about whether to become pregnant or not. That choice is for teenagers, whom I taught in high school, to become sexually active or not to be sexually active.
If a person does make the choice to be sexually active and they do become pregnant, then they have further choices open to them. Certainly, there is the adoption option, whether to keep the child or whether to have an abortion, but the choice is not just one choice, whether to have an abortion or not.
I will be voting for the amendments which strengthen this bill in favour of protection for the unborn and against the idea of psychological health, because it is so nebulous. I will be voting in favour of Motions Nos. 4, 22,

May 23, 1990
Government Orders
5, 10, 12, 13, 14, 16, and, if 16 is defeated, then 17A as well as 19.
I know that many people are wishing to speak on this debate. I certainly admire the calibre of debate that has taken place in this chamber. In my year and a half here as a member, this is the bill to which the most respect has been paid. I appreciate that.
I would like to close off with a verse of scripture because we in Canada call ourselves a Christian nation, one that was founded on Christian principles. I believe that this sums it up when we are worried about the semantics of where life really begins. I think it is fairly clear when the psalmist David wrote in Psalm 139, verses 13 through 16:
Thou hast covered me in my mother's womb - I will praise thee, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. My substance was not hid from thee when I was made in secret-Thine eyes did see my substance, yet being unperfect; and in thy book all my members were written, which in continuance were fashioned, when as yet there was none of them.
I think it is very clear from that that life does begin at conception. I am pro-choice. I choose life.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to say a few words on Bill C-43 today.
I want to say at the outset, and make my position absolutely clear, that I support a woman's right to make a decision on whether or not she should terminate a pregnancy, and that that decision should be made between her and a doctor.
It is not a question that should be subject to legislation. In fact, if it should be a subject of any legislation, then I would make the argument that it should fall under the Canada Health Act. Once a woman has made that conscious decision to terminate a pregnancy, and once it has been agreed upon by her personal doctor, between both of them, then she should have access to proper medical treatment.
I am proud to take that position. I did not arrive at that conclusion today. I arrived at it many years ago and made my position absolutely clear in numerous election campaigns in my constituency of Beaches-Woodbine. Any time I was asked at all-candidates meetings or elsewhere I made it absolutely clear that that was my position.
I do not want to deal with the legalities. I think there has been far too much debate about the legalities involved. It is a basic question of human rights and especially the rights of women.
If this government were serious about trying to minimize the number of abortions in this country, it would do things other than cut back on programs which actually encourage abortions to take place.
Starting with the previous government and since this government came to power, there have been reductions to family allowance programs and the clawback of benefits. There have been reductions in funding for women's programs. There have been drastic reductions in family planning and family counselling programs. All of those programs have been cut, as well as the child care program for which this government promised to increase funding but has never come through on.
I do not doubt the sincerity of people who hold a position opposite to mine. I respect such a point of view, even though I do not share it, because this is a deeply moral issue for many people. I accept that. I do not necessarily agree with them, but I at least accept it.
There is an argument which is continually being made, mainly by men, but I have heard it made by women, that if a woman chooses to become pregnant, she has to carry that child through conception to birth because she allowed herself to get pregnant. It has been a long time since a woman got herself pregnant. It seems to me that there are two people responsible for that pregnancy.
I could make an equally strong argument that the weight of responsibility lies with the man, not with the woman. When I hear members like the member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell suggest that the penalty for anyone contravening this legislation should be increased from two years in prison to 20 years in prison based on specious arguments that compare a pregnant woman to someone in a speedboat hauling someone along on a pair of water skis, it is simply not acceptable to me. There is no comparison. I am trying to keep the rhetoric low, but I think it is a stupid argument and it displays something about the approach that some people bring to this debate. I think it lowers the level of debate.
May 23, 1990

The question before this House and before the country in 1990 should be whether or not a woman is a piece of property. This bill continues the argument that women are property.
Give me a break.

The hon. member asks me to give him a break. I am trying to give him a break. I am trying to keep the debate on a level of some truth. If the hon. member wants to get up and dispute what I am saying, let him do it, but to sit there and heckle me for making a statement is not acceptable to me. Get on your feet and tell us what you think.
I did.

Well, get up again. You will have another opportunity, and then I will respond to you, my friend.
The question is whether in 1990 a woman is viewed as being a person responsible enough to make a decision on her own. I think she is. This bill, by placing abortion back in the Criminal Code, is going to be making criminals out of an awful lot of women and an awful lot of people in the medical profession. I would put money on it that in a few years from now we will be faced with a larger problem than we are today without this bill.
I will be voting against the amendments before the House today except for Motion No. 24. I do not agree that any of the amendments which have been put forward will help women who find themselves with an unwanted pregnancy. I think probably Motion No. 24 would do that. If we have to live with this bill-which I certainly hope we will not have to-then I would adopt Motion No. 24 to get rid of it because that is what Motion No. 24 will do.
When that amendment comes before the House this evening I urge members to vote in favour of Motion No. 24, and defeat the rest of them.

Mr. Speaker, this is a very difficult and thorny issue that pleases no one. It is difficult to resolve, whichever side of the issue you find yourself on. The minister said that a delicate balance was what was required.
I originally voiced my opinion on this bill when it was first tabled. I said that there were very serious flaws in it. However, in the democratic process in which we are
Government Orders
fortunate enough to live, I voted that the bill go to a legislative committee for serious study and evaluation. At that time groups which were particularly concerned, including women, medical practitioners and families could be heard so that we would be able to bring forward amendments that would improve the bill. We could then decide if the minister's view, that putting this in the Criminal Code would be the only way to ensure access and to ensure fair payment with respect to a medical procedure, that a woman would have the right to choose, if she so desired.
At that time I considered that the bill was flawed. However, I thought that we had the obligation to send it to a legislative committee. It was sent to a legislative committee. The government has indicated that it is not interested in any kind of amendments. It is resisting all amendments saying that they would unbalance the very delicate compromise that has been found in this bill. It is not prepared to consider any kind of amendment.
A woman's right to choice, her right to consult a doctor, which I consider to be very important, not for his permission but for his advice and guidance so that she could make an enlightened decision was what was important when this bill was studied in the legislative committee. I do not believe that what was heard is faithfully reflected in the kind of amendments that we have before us. The majority of these amendments are very one-sided.
I am concerned about the constitutionality of this bill. I recall for you, Mr. Speaker, the opinion that was expressed by Chief Justice Brian Dickson of the Supreme Court on the Morgentaler case, which struck down the old abortion law. He said that forcing a woman by threat of criminal sanction to carry a foetus to term unless she meets certain criteria unrelated to her own priorities and aspirations is a profound interference with a woman's body and thus an infringement on security of the person.
I do not believe that this bill would meet a test of constitutionality. I also believe that where the foetus needs some protection-and that was also indicated in the decision of the court-that protection is not to be found in this bill.
A woman's right to choice, not permission, a woman's right to make decisions on her own reproductive obligations has been a conflict which has been present

May 23, 1990
Government Orders
throughout history. It indicates that abortions will happen. If you close the door to any kind of option, you can be sure that we will be back into some very serious medical health problems. We have been without an abortion bill, or without any constraints on access to the right to terminate a pregnancy if a woman wishes, and we have not seen an increase in any abortions. Ninety-nine per cent of those abortions take place before 12 weeks.
I think that we are going to have to trust women. I think women deserve to be trusted. They will make the right choice. I would say to you, Mr. Speaker, that the number and spacing of children in a society that is free of violence, free of abuse, free from hunger, free from poverty, free from rape and incest are all factors that families take into consideration, but the final decision must be that of a woman in consultation with her doctor. She makes the final decision.
Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, I do not see anything in this bill that would ensure, either through the Canada Health Act or the Criminal Code, the kinds of things that I feel are necessary to enable a woman to enjoy and rejoice in the pregnancy and in the anticipation of a child being added to her life. This is not found in this bill.
I would suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the threat of legal action, which could persuade many doctors to stop performing abortions and many women to fear ending up as criminals within our criminal justice system, does not answer the needs of this society.
The delicate balance has not been found. We have not found the proper kind of accommodation. Respect for constitutional guarantees has not been tested or found in this bill. Respect for individual rights and freedom of personal decision is not found in this bill. Because these issues have not been addressed, I would choose to vote against all amendments at this time and I will certainly vote against the bill at third reading.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to say that I too will vote against this bill on third reading, as I did on second reading, and as I did on first reading.
The only possible amendment I can see myself supporting is that amendment of my colleague in the New Democratic Party for New Westminster-Burnaby.
I stand here, Mr. Speaker, feeling sad about what we are doing. I am unhappy about the way the government is treating Canadian women. Perhaps I should not be surprised, but I was one of those members who considered Bill C-43 in the legislative committee. We listened to women from every province and territory in this country. We listened to cries from the heart from these women. We heard stories of horror about conditions that women and children are forced to live in. We heard stories that would have been laughable were they not so sad, about the lack of access to medical care, the lack of access to proper contraception, the lack of access to proper education, the lack of access to a social service support network.
What was painted for us in that committee was a Canada that is not friendly to women and particularly not friendly to the children that we have within our care today.
I recall very clearly the presentation to the committee of Shirley Carr of the Canadian Labour Congress. She said to us: "I was here 25 years ago making the same plea. I cannot believe that we have progressed so little that I am back again 25 years later saying the same things".
This bill is an insult to both sides. On one hand, it says that abortion is illegal. On the other hand, it says that here is an exception so large that anyone who is prepared to make a few concessions here and there about what is actually going on will be able to slide through. Canadian women do not want to concoct stories. They do not want to have to worry that someone, a neighbour, a disgruntled ex-husband, a disgruntled boyfriend will lay a charge over something as personal and as personally agonizing as the question of whether or not to terminate a pregnancy.
Another thing I think women on the legislative committee had in common was the idea that if one is in favour of a woman's right to control her own body, to self-determination, that one is pro-abortion. Let that phrase be thrown out now and forever. The majority of Canadians who support the option for choice are not pro-abortion. We all know that, as an option, abortion is

May 23, 1990

a last resort. It is one with which no one is happy. It is one with which no one is comfortable. It is one that Canadian women wish they did not have to choose.
If this country were all it could be, abortion is an option that Canadian women would rarely, if ever, choose.
The polarization that this debate has created leaves women and children as victims. We expend time and energy arguing the question of abortion and choice and arguing legislation brought forward, and we spend time and money on committees et cetera. These are energies of people who must come forward to speak to committies which would be far better spent in solving the social problems that create the need for abortion. Nobody in this chamber is going to be prepared to say that poverty or child and wife abuse do not exist in this country. We know they do. All too frequently we see incidents of this. Violence in the family against women and children is something that is a norm in Canadian life.
I do not think anyone in this Chamber would have the temerity to rise and suggest that as a society we properly educate our children or our citizenry in general on sexuality, on responsibility or on what it is to maintain adult relationships, giving them the proper intellectual wherewithal to choose when to begin them.
Nobody, after sitting in the legislative committee and listening to the lack of access to proper medical care across the country suffered by so many women, could possibly say that women can make a choice freely in our society as it exists today.
Contraception is not adequate for vast numbers of Canadian women. Education in sexuality has left many women and children short of the mark in knowing what it is they must do. The lack of facilities has left them, in many regions of the country, with an inability to get the facilities and the contraception they need.
With those situations existing, the option of abortion for many is the only option. I heard the expression from one of the witnesses that if you make your bed, then you must lie in it and this was said with sort of a sneer. It is absolutely unbelievable to me in 1990 that we still treat women and children in the manner in which we do, and that we still look at situations of human misery as ones where punishment must be inflicted. Canadian women know what they need and what is necessary to ensure
Government Orders
that our society is fair and just. They know that they do not have it.
Whatever happens with this law, it will not change one thing. While social problems exist, such as violence against women and children, and a lack of care in our society for those who need it, then abortion will exist.
The only question to be answered by individual members of the House when they vote is whether abortion will be performed in a safe medical facility or whether it will exist outside these safeguards, because no legislation will stop abortion while society condones the treatment of women and children that we see before us today. Violence against women has been part of our history and that, sadly, will be part of our future. The only question we have to ask is, do you want abortion performed in a safe situation or do you want it performed in an unsafe situation?
I suggest that these amendments do nothing to improve the situation for women and children in this country. These amendments, if passed, will do nothing to improve a bill which is a flawed and unacceptable piece of legislation.
I suggest that the Government of Canada leave these decisions to the women of Canada, but that the Government of Canada take the necessary steps to create a climate wherein the women of Canada can make these choices freely, with the proper knowledge, the proper equipment and in a proper atmosphere which gives dignity and value to human life. If we do not treat the lives we have on this earth and in this country with dignity, then there is no reason to suppose that women who give life will want to do so.

Mr. Speaker, after 22 years in the House, this is the third time I have spoken on this issue. One wonders when society in general and successive governments in particular will take action that will substantially reduce, if not eliminate, the demand or the perceived need for an abortion.
I do not support abortion on demand totally, and I have said so frequently. I oppose it as a method of birth control or as an irresponsible solution for misbehaviour. That is a choice which I have made myself and one that each of us has to make individually.

May 23, 1990
Government Orders
I say to my pro-life colleagues that I respect their views and deeply held convictions. But, to merely sit still and wring your hands and tinker with legal machinery is not opposition. That is blind adherence to a dogma. Making abortions legal or illegal does nothing toward solving the problem-and witness prohibition outlawing liquor which did not stop people from drinking.
Canada's social structure is presently so poorly balanced that it invites violence of which abortion can be seen as one form. It is in redressing this inequality that I and my colleagues are engaged. Ultimately, a just society will have fewer invitations to this kind of violence. I have constantly fought and worked for, as my colleagues have, legislation to support troubled families and unduly burdened women so that the real or perceived need to resort to abortion will become obsolete.
It seems to me that women do not resort to abortion just because they suddenly do not love babies. It is because they find themselves caught in a frightening and terrifying squeeze: no housing, no job, no husband, no help, no acceptance, no love, no support.
I hope with the work of all of us in the House of Commons that we can restructure society to make it hospitable to life so that any child brought into this world would not go wanting or be so disadvantaged that no one would want to undertake that child's sustenance. To decry abortion without the restructuring of society is to beat the air. We must have wide-sweeping reforms favouring social security for single parent families and other poor families. Do not talk to me about immorality. When government shows-this one and the preceding ones-the immorality of refusing to implement legislation on child care, it is an immorality that invites abortions.
We must have more affordable and accessible child care centres so that parents continue both their work and their education. We must have a legal requirement for every employer in Canada to provide for a minimum of two years' leave of absence for an employee who is becoming a new parent, with a real guarantee that that employee can return to the same or a better position with that employer.
Chartered banks must be directed to use a significant part of their funds to lower mortgage loans so that housing costs will no longer cripple young families struggling to make ends meet. Medicare of which we in
Saskatchewan are so proud must be strengthened and must become a norm for society all over Canada and the world. Federal funding must be available to the provinces to educate about all forms of birth control, starting in the schools, to encourage responsibility and decrease the ignorance that exists on the subject. Then each person may be informed and intelligently adopt a method of birth control that best meets one's own religious beliefs, economic situation, and family needs. There are, in short, many massive social changes that have to be made before we will see the day that the recourse to abortion is no longer the evident way out. There is much to be done. My colleagues and I invite all my colleagues in the government and the Official Opposition to join in redressing our social ills. The New Democratic Party is not interested in defending the wealthy. They have always been able to find an abortion somewhere, and I have had experience with that. We, on the contrary, are very concerned with helping those whom society has so shortchanged or ignores such that all other hope seems to have expired.
The statement of April 1973 by the Canadian Catholic Conference of Bishops has been of great help to me, and I want to quote it:
To be involved in the task of making this society hospitable to life is a foremost requirement of social justice. That is why we must take most seriously the rebuke that those who oppose abortion care too little about the special problems of mothers and the burdens of rearing children once they are born.
If respect for life seems to end with birth, our perceptions and values are truncated and incomplete. The call of Christ, that we should bear one another's burdens, demands that we reach out in practical ways to share all the burdens of parenthood. The indicated aid and support will include working to change economic and social realities in the direction of justice and respect for life. From doing this, we must not flinch.
Whatever law we have-and I would prefer we have none-must be equally enforced. Hospitals which are funded by taxpayers' dollars should provide the services the law allows.
When society demands and all levels of government implement the measures I have illustrated-and there are many others-then I believe we will see a dramatic reduction in the number of abortions; not a reduction because women will go somewhere else to have an abortion, but because thousands of Canadian women will no longer need to resort to abortion as the best or only avenue left open to them. They will have a real choice,
May 23, 1990

and though I am pro-choice, what kind of a choice do they have?
I ask my pro-life colleagues what a retarded 16 year old girl from a poor family made pregnant by a 19 year old brother is supposed to do? She has no help. What about a 15 year old girl made pregnant by a drunken father? What is she supposed to do? What is a woman made pregnant after a beating and a rape by a husband or other attacker, I ask my pro-life friends, supposed to do? Don't say adoption, because I can take you to a home in Regina to see a woman who should be a saint. She is looking after six children, two of whom are vegetables, no one will adopt. When I challenged the pro-life groups in my city that came to see me in my office on numerous occasions-and I always showed them the courtesy of hearing them out and meeting with them-to go to that home with me and adopt them, they said: "We will find some way to have them looked after". That is hypocrisy of the worst kind.
May I say in closing that while hundreds of thousands of kids in this country are homeless or hungry, we have no business passing legislation such as this. I will vote against all the amendments except Motion No. 24, and I will vote against the bill.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to say a few words on Bill C-43. As you know, it is not my custom to be talkative in the chamber, although I participate a lot in committee work. This is one bill before the House on which I think most members want to say something on this occasion.
I want to explain my position a little by indicating that I am neither from the classical pro-choice side nor the classical pro-life side. My position on abortion is somewhere in between. I listened to my colleague from Regina-Lumsden and I agreed with a number of points he made, although I do not think we see eye to eye on the subject.
As a nation and a government we should try to prevent the need for abortion by trying to give parents the education and the opportunity to take steps that preclude anyone wishing to have an abortion. This is the ideal way, obviously. I think that governments over the
Government Orders
years have failed to implement policies to the extent that they might to move in that direction.
Having said what is my position, as a physician I have been acquainted with the issue of abortions in a practical way having been involved with them from time to time. I must say that over the years, the longer I spend in the House, the more closely I come to the pro-life side, to the extent that I feel we should do all we can to discourage abortions when possible.
I was interested enough in this whole issue that when there was difficulty coming to a conclusion as to what kind of law we should have in this country and what kind of bills that come before the House, I was pleased to participate with other colleagues on the government side in a unique committee which came up with the bill that is before the House now, Bill C-43.
In spite of the fact that I would like to see abortions discouraged to the extent that is humanly possible, I would like to indicate my support for Bill C-43 for several reasons. I happen to believe that it is probably preferable to have some law in this nation that does indicate some concern and protection for the foetus. As I understand the interpretations given by the Supreme Court, I think the message we got from it too was that there was reason this Parliament might want to see some protection for the foetus. I can see that possibly that may well be coming down the road.
I had a lot of soul-searching to do with this bill. It is somewhat like the bills on capital punishment. I was involved in those two debates as well back in 1975 or 1976 and again more recently. Although those were bills that called for a free vote, as it were, they were slightly different. One could vote either for or against capital punishment, but here we are not voting for or against abortion. There are many situations in between. I see that the majority of Canadians, by the pollings that were done, are certainly in between this issue. The majority prefer not to be in the pure classic pro-life position or in the pure pro-choice position.
I was very impressed by what was done by the committee that was put together to bring forward a consensus on the bill before the House. It was co-chaired by two people. In terms of their own personal convictions, one was strongly pro-life and the other was strongly prochoice. To see those co-chairpersons and representatives

May 23, 1990
Government Orders
from various parts of the spectrum between the pro-life and pro-choice sides come together as a group and come up with Bill C-43 was very impressive.
I have actually had a number of representations from constituents. I have had many sincere letters, telephone calls and petitions from those who represent the pro-life side of this issue. I respect their position very deeply. I know how sincere they are about it. I know from whence they come and the source of their strong convictions based on religious background, training and scruples which I respect.
I am convinced that the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada was such that if we came up with a bill that would represent what it wanted us to do, we would probably find that law to be ruled unconstitutional when it was challenged and brought to the Supreme Court of Canada.
What impressed me the most was something I read recently in one of the journals that comes into our house. It is called Contact and is put out by people who have a very strong Christian conviction. The heading of an article on the front page of a recent edition read: "Christians urged to support pro-life abortion law amendments." The staff of the Calvanistic Contact wrote this article, but they quote extensively from Mr. Gerald Vandezande who is the public affairs director for Citizens for Public Justice, CPJ. They have been quoted here in the House previously during this debate.
I happen to know a bit of the background of Mr. Gerald Vandezande because he comes out of my constituency. I know his parents and I know the strong convictions that he and his family and others who belong to the same church as he belongs to in my area adhere to. I respect him very deeply. In fact, my wife comes out of that same tradition as well and I have a strong conviction for their position.
I want to read part of this article which impressed me. As I indicated, Mr. Vandezande is the public affairs director for Citizens for Public Justice and knowing him to be a committed pro-life person, he shows some insight which I think supports my position in favour of this bill. I want to quote from this article because I think it has some bearing on this issue. I am quoting now from the
article, not from what he said, although he is being paraphrased by the staff writer of this particular article:
At issue is whether Canada will have a law governing abortions or not. If Bill C-43 is defeated, with or without some of the proposed amendments, Parliament is likely to give up trying to bring forward an abortion bill.
I believe that to be true, Mr. Speaker. The article further states:
Christians may need to decide, says Vandezande, whether the bill now before Parliament is better than no abortion law at all.
This is something I have raised with many of my pro-life people, whether or not we should have no bill at all. When I am challenged to vote against this bill, I say that we may then have no bill at all. I happen to agree with what Mr. Vandezande is saying here, namely, that we have to decide whether the bill now before Parliament is better than no abortion law at all.
The article goes on for another sentence or two and states:
CPJ is urging all Christians to phone or write their MP - to vote for the most life-affirming legislation and social policy measures possible today.
I want to emphasize those last two words. He is calling upon us as Christians, calling upon Christians in Canada, to phone and write to us as MPs asking us "to vote for the most life-affirming legislation and social policy measures possible today".
It is my conviction, after sitting on the committee that came up with this bill, that this is the only bill that is going to gain the support of this House.
If the bill is amended either way, either on the pro-choice side or the pro-life side, it is going to be defeated and we will then have no bill at all.
I feel very strongly and I feel very much encouraged that somebody who comes from a very strong pro-life position has the courage and has the insight, I would have to say, to recognize the predicament that we as parliamentarians are in, and if we want to have any bill at all, and I think some bill is better than no bill, it is essential that we vote for Bill C-43.
Based on that, it is my intention this evening when the vote is called to vote against all the amendments, and come third reading of the bill, I will want to support it because I feel it is the one bill that will possibly and hopefully sustain the support of this House.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few comments on listening to the hon. member's presentation, a person over the years in whom I have had a great deal of confidence in his judgement and opinion. I do take exception to the statements made in the House concerning the legislation before us on the abortion issue.
I do not believe that this is a consensus bill at all, nor does anyone in the party that I represent. I think many of the members of the government are very upset with this particular piece of legislation. It is not a compromise. It is probably the worst choice that could have been made.
I am absolutely astounded that a bill could come before this House and generate the antipathy of both sides, that a bill could be presented in this House and be absolutely opposed by both the anti-choice and the pro-choice forces in this country. I would point out to the member that this bill is not better than not having a bill. This is a bad bill. The people who drafted it, presented it to this House, forced it on the government members and the Cabinet and are attempting to sell it as, a compromise, are doing a great disservice to this House.
We have missed the mark as legislators. The price we will pay is that in the next federal election we will be tom to pieces on the platform, as both sides of the issue, who will be completely dissatisfied with this, will carry this issue on. This Parliament is not finished with this issue because it is a bad bill.
All but one of the amendments are bad amendments. Virtually all of my colleagues have stood in this House to oppose the amendments that basically curtail the choice of women on an absolutely fundamental issue. It is wrong. I will vote against every single one of the amendments except the one proposed by my colleague from New Westminster-Burnaby. In the end I will vote against this bill.
It is my hope that other colleagues on all sides of this House will join myself and other members who believe this legislation is very detrimental to the work of Parliament and, indeed, to women in Canada and that they will also vote against this bill.
